maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at 10.30 last night I had almost completed my remarks but had not quite finished. Before I proceed I should like to make a correction in the reporting of something I said about the gasoline tax last night. Either it was a slip of the tongue on my part or an error in reporting. As found on page 6633 of Hansard, I am reported as having said:
-let us consider the tax on gasoline. In Prince Edward Island it is 18 cents a gallon. There are only two other provinces with a gasoline tax that high, namely. Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
What I meant to say was that there are only two provinces with higher gasoline taxes, namely Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, the tax in those provinces being 19 cents a gallon. In New Brunswick the tax is also 18 cents a gallon, but the other six provinces of Canada have lower rates of gasoline tax.
I was pointing out last night that Prince Edward Island feels it will be getting less than it deserves and less than its rightful share of the increased payments to the provinces provided by the bill. I hope this is in no way due to the myopic view of the economic problems of the maritimes which the Minister of Finance has exhibited on occasion in the past. I am not naive enough to believe that anything I say at this stage will bring about any material change in the bill, but I appeal to the minister once more to reconsider the adjustment as far as Prince Edward Island is concerned in case some improvement could be made.
Failing that I want to make one suggestion to the government with reference to shared cost programs. On their face, shared cost programs seem to be a bargain as far as the provinces are concerned when, for instance, the federal government offers to pay a fixed percentage of a roads program or something of that sort. Unfortunately, however, as the minister well knows, something one cannot afford is not a bargain at any price. These shared cost programs may be well and good for provinces that have a good taxation base and can reasonably raise their share of the costs involved, but in the case of provinces where the tax base is now exploited almost


as far as it is practicable it is very difficult for them to pay their share of these fixed charges.
I suggest to the government that consideration should be given to these shared cost programs. I suggest that in future the percentage of the shared cost programs to be paid by each province should be in proportion to that province's ability to pay. In other words the share of the federal government should be in proportion to the equalization payments made to each province; otherwise a proportionately greater load is placed on the poorer provinces, thus throwing their future budgeting completely out of balance.
Now, lest the minister misinterprets the general trend of my remarks, let me say I am not advocating bigger and bigger raids on the federal treasury by the provinces. I realize fully the great responsibility under which the minister labours.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Order, please. May I bring to the attention of the members of the committee the fact it is rather noisy, and that is unfair to the hon. member who has the floor at the moment.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I realize the great responsibility that is placed on the shoulders of any minister of finance of this country under present conditions of increasing public debt generally, increasing demands for further public services, the general growth and expansion in our country and the growing need for the expansion of public works, using that terms in the broad sense. However, I believe it is time that we Canadians faced up to some of our responsibilities so far as our financial position as a nation is concerned.
I am directing these remarks to all levels of government. It is a fallacy for any level of government to believe it can get whatever it needs from another level of government, and that this is free. The taxpayers who have to pay the shot in the end are the same Canadian people, regardless of what level of government makes the expenditure.
Now, I am not advocating the ultra strict situation that is expressed in the constitution of some of the states of the United States under which they are not allowed to go into debt at all in some cases, while in other cases they cannot go into debt without having a referendum. I do believe that making public expenditures, creating debts, by all levels of government represents good

business procedure If the money is invested in valid national assets.
On the other hand, I do not approve of the careless attitude which is sometimes expressed in some circles that you do not have to worry at all about public debt; it is the generations yet unborn that will have to pay for it anyway. The feeling is that, in effect, you just phone the money number, as it were, and let somebody else worry about the debt when its liquidation becomes necessary. I think we have to look carefully at the debts we hand on to posterity. There certainly will be a very large national debt handed on to generations yet unborn, but that is valid provided we also hand on comparable national assets to offset those debts.
I am considerably worried, though, about the snowballing effect of public expenditure at all levels of government, and in this connection I would take as an example one of our public corporations which parliament has spent very little time considering in the past few years. I refer to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation just by way of illustration. I am not saying these expenditures are necessarily wrong; I am using them as an example of the tremendous increase which has come about in expenditures.
In the year 1963-64 the C.B.C. spent $115 milion, in round figures, 70 per cent of which was paid by the government or a total of almost $81 million just to make up the deficit of the C.B.C. alone. As recently as the fiscal year 1907-08 the total budget of the federal government for all services was only $76 million. The C.B.C. costs the taxpayers more in a year now than it took to run this whole country in 1908.
I am concerned, too, about the very rapid increase in our debt at all levels of government, and I should like to briefly quote some figures for the information of this committee. In 1942 the total debt of all the provincial governments was less than $2 billion. By 1952 it was well over $3 billion and by 1960 it was over $7 billion. The federal debt in 1932 was less than $3 billion. In 1942 it was almost $7 billion and in 1952 it was over $11 billion. By 1960 it had reached $26 billion. In 1960 the total municipal debt in Canada was almost $5 billion, so that by 1960 we had a total public debt amounting to $38 billion, or about $2,000 in respect of every man, woman and child in Canada.
I am not saying this is necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the Canadian people should consider whether or not they have assets to balance this huge debt, assets in the form
Federal-Provincial Relations of public utilities and facilities resulting from these capital expenditures, such as roads and everything else which go to make possible the development of a country. If we have those assets, the situation is good. If we do not, we should watch very carefully that we are not overspending recklessly.
Having said that, I wish to conclude my remarks; but before doing so I should like to make one more appeal to the minister to examine carefully the formulae in this bill, because I think they produce an effect which is not entirely fair-relatively, that is-to the province from which I come, namely Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
This debate, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has pointed out, has been the occasion for a number of good statements in the best parliamentary tradition. Some excellent observations have been made on the whole question of federal-provincial relations.
I think we have all become aware, in the period since 1945, that the requirements at provincial and municipal levels of government in Canada for additional sources of revenues to carry out their obligations in respect to such fields as education and highways, to name only two, have expanded very rapidly indeed. The present legislation recognizes this need, but it also goes as far as it is possible for the federal government to go, in my opinion, in terms of making concessions to recognize provincial requirements for more revenues.
There is a great deal of talk these days about the constitution and constitutional responsibilities. One of the things that frighten me is the degree to which a series of myths are gaining acceptance by the people who do not always look at the record and the facts. The first myth runs in these terms: since the second world war there has been a huge, bureaucratic, centralizing government which has strangled the life out of the provinces. It has become fashionable in many quarters to decry centralization and to plead the cause of provincial autonomy.
What people forget is that the wartime agreements eliminated a tax jungle of confused municipal sales taxes, provincial sales taxes, federal sales taxes, income taxes and so on. The tax rental agreements which eventually emerged provided for a national system which, in turn, made possible national development. What we must not forget is that those years since 1945 have been years of unparalleled growth; growth in population, growth in gross national product and growth in per
6654	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Relations capita incomes. All provinces have shared in this growth, although some of them particularly the Atlantic provinces, have not shared as much as the others.
In this period the federal government did carry out several basic functions which in my opinion were absolutely essential for the continued growth and prosperity of Canada. On the whole, fiscal and monetary policies were followed which were appropriate for Canada's development. Vigorous trade expansion took place. Canada's representatives participated in conferences abroad with a well founded confidence that the government they represented could carry out the commitments made in Canada's name. Trade and commercial policy, monetary policy, protection of the Canadian dollar, policies concerning national development relating to our frontiers, our resources; these were all possible. Along with them went a tax structure that had a great deal of logic to it and went a long way toward minimizing overlapping of jurisdictions and unnecessary confusion.
These were good years. There is not a member of this house who will rise and say that our record of growth and development would not compare favourably with that of any other part of the world. In my opinion you are not a centralist when you say the federal government must protect its money and banking powers, must control immigration, and must represent Canada not only in external relations but also in trade and development policies with other nations of the commonwealth and the world. These powers are the essence of the federal function, and they cannot be destroyed.
At the other end of the scale there are functions which are clearly provincial. These included such fields as education, property and civic rights. There is no thought of the federal government taking any measures which would disturb the independence of a minority group or groups. Firm guarantees were written into our constitution years ago, and these must be respected.
Just as there is no serious thought of the federal government taking over provincial responsibilities, it would be equally disturbing to our national growth and prosperity for the provincial authorities to undermine federal powers. Canada could not have ten currencies, or ten trade policies, or ten immigration policies. Interregional and interprovincial barriers to trade must be resisted at all costs. There have been a number of speeches made on this aspect, including some by hon. members opposite.


There is, however, a large grey area between those powers which are exclusively federal and those which are exclusively provincial. This is the area where confusion has arisen on almost a continuous basis since 1867, and where our new concepts of cooperative federalism have most to offer. This area is perhaps well illustrated by health and welfare grants-

speechtext:
This area is perhaps well illustrated by health and welfare grants, where the principle of shared cost grants by the federal government to programs which are provincially operated has been steadily developed. It is fashionable in some quarters today to take all these arrangements and say that the federal government must get out of hospital insurance, health grants and unemployment assistance, blindness allowances, disabled persons allowances and old age assistance.
The difficulty with this approach is that the provinces which wish the federal government to leave these fields insist, quite understandably, upon compensation by way of additional revenue sources or additional tax abatement. The principle of opting out has been developed to provide compensatory grants to provinces that will not choose to participate in the shared cost programs. The present measure before us, for example, provides for an additional tax abatement of 3 per cent for those provinces not participating in the youth allowances program.
The problem here relates to how far tax abatement can go. In the present legislation the federal government will derive only 25 cents out of every dollar collected in succession duties. What will this mean when the problem of the amendment of succession duties legislation is considered? Any proposal to decrease succession duties-I admit that we do not often decrease taxes these days, but it

is conceivable that we might-could conceivably involve prior discussions at a federal-provincial conference. If we commit ourselves to such a degree that flexibility in regard to taxation by the federal government is impaired, then one basic federal function will have been destroyed.
The Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings both commented in the course of this debate that they were worried about the limited scope left to the Minister of Finance in relation to the job which he has to do. The Minister of Finance made it quite clear in the debate that he is convinced he has ample authority to do what he considers necessary. In my opinion the authority of the Minister of Finance cannot be curtailed any further than it has been, and I do hope that the annual conferences with the provincial ministers which are anticipated, from the remarks of the Minister of Finance, will not move into the field of detailed administration of federal succession duties or federal income tax legislation.
The Minister of Finance has been kind enough to make available to me some rough calculations of the effect of tax abatement on personal income taxes if the provinces choose to contract out of hospital insurance, hospital construction, health grants, old age assistance, blindness allowances, disabled persons allowances and unemployment assistance. If an equalized procedure is adopted in tax abatement, an additional 18 per cent might be involved for the province of Quebec on top of the 27 per cent which would be automatic, in the legislation now under consideration, for 1966. In other words a total of 45 per cent of personal income tax might be abated, assuming an equalized approach. If equalization is not adopted, an even greater percentage of tax abatement would be involved.
There has been discussion relating to some of these matters, but to the best of my knowledge and belief no other shared cost program has been under this type of discussion by spokesmen for the government. However, the premier of the province of Quebec last December made reference to opting out of the old age security program, and from my own calculations this would involve an additional 20 per cent. If we were to accept this kind of proposal- and I do not think any responsible group is suggesting this-in regard to family allowances also, something in excess of 80 per cent of income taxes might be involved.
Federal-Provincial Relations
It is abundantly clear that there is a limit to how far tax abatement can be adopted by the federal government on the opting out principle. If the provincial stake were to exceed 50 per cent, then the federal position would become difficult indeed. Up to the present point, so far as I am aware, no province has raised the question of participation in discussions on actual federal tax rates, probably because the percentage of tax abatement has been relatively small. I note from the press, however, that the conference of provincial premiers has raised a question of procedure for collection of each other's sales taxes, and a serious constitutional question is raised as to how far the provincial authorities can interfere with the federal powers. So far in this house we have heard a tremendous volume of complaint about federal intervention in provincial rights. I think it is equally valid to say to the provincial authorities, "Canada cannot exist as a nation if you undermine certain basic federal responsibilities in money and banking, currency and national development".
The over-all national rate of economic development must depend on federal policy. Basic to national development is the avoidance of a national tax jungle and, in this area, the federal contribution should not be subjected to any self denying act on the part of this parliament. As an easterner, for example, I deplore very much the attempt of the premier of British Columbia to set up his own bank. Surely banking and currency is a federal matter. I do not believe that the extension of provincial powers into certain federal functions is in the interests of Canada, and I believe it would lead to the impoverishment of every one of us if it were pursued relentlessly, as some quarters would have us do.
We all know that the key to responsibility is in the tax power and the allocation of revenues. The bill before us at present goes a long way to meeting the requests of the provincial authorities and, in my opinion, this is just as far as any federal government can go. There should be no question whatsoever of the federal ability to raise and lower taxes, to incur deficits or surpluses in accordance with what is considered to be appropriate for the particular stage of the business cycle in which we find ourselves. This ability cannot be compromised. If a federal-provincial conference must precede every change in the succession duties or the personal income tax, then the ability to carry out basic fiscal policy will have been seriously impaired.

Federal-Provincial Relations
There is still another reason why we must think carefully before agreeing to a general extension of the opting out formula. The shared cost programs were a means of achieving minimum national standards in areas where confusion would otherwise have reigned. In hospital insurance, for example, each province worked out its own program. There are great variations in methods of financing programs, in administration and in the type of services provided through hospitals from one province to another in Canada. When each province signed an agreement with the federal government, however, as a result of which they received federal participation funds, they agreed to provide as insured service, hospital care at the standard ward level, to eliminate discriminatory charges and make provision to accept people who moved from one province to another without subjecting them to waiting periods. They also agreed to use uniform accounting procedures and a uniform basis of statistical reporting.
The shared cost programs recognized regional and provincial diversity but left the essential administration in provincial hands, and maintained at the same time a procedure for regular conferences of officials and the achievement of national minimum standards. These standards were achieved with the advice of conferences and through agreements in the general field of shared cost programs.
One cannot help but ask, what would opting out in health grants and hospital insurance do to the dominion council of health which meets every six months? How would its agenda be affected? Would provincial officials still confer regularly on their problems and try to deal with them in the same orderly way, exchanging experiences from the Atlantic to the Pacific in Canada? If Quebec, for example-again-opts out, who will be the spokesman for the French language hospitals and institutions at the federal conference table? Could a province which opts out still insist on its right to participate in the discussions relating to the administration of the non-opting out provinces? If Quebec were to opt out from a wide range of the health and welfare programs, could a federal minister from Quebec be responsible for that department in this house? These questions are very fundamental and are still unanswered.
A second myth of our time, which has been perpetuated by responsible people, relates to the revision of our constitution. Just a few weeks ago in this house we passed


a resolution asking the parliament of the United Kingdom to, in effect, amend our constitution so the federal authority could legislate for pensions with survivor benefits. I think spokesmen for every party in this house at that time rose and said how humiliating it was to have to go to the parliament of another country to amend our constitution, to ask for this permission.
It is quite clear why we must do this. The rule of unanimity of the ten provinces has been upheld, and not least by the province of Quebec, because that province fears that we cannot agree upon a procedure for amending our own constitution which will at the same time give to those of the French language and culture the minority protection that they have every right to expect. I do not blame or criticize the province for this fear; it is their right to insist on safeguards. Just for this reason our constitution cannot be amended here, and we must undergo the humiliating experience of asking someone else to change it for us.
I cannot help but contrast this with the speech made, for example, by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue on July 13, when he added his voice to the chorus being raised for a constitutional amendment. The same hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue denounced co-operative federalism in strong terms but had a rather grudging admiration for the contracting out or the opting out principle. I am not surprised at this, because it seems to me that the group he represents on that side of the house is in the process of opting out or contracting out from its own party. I think the full constitutional implications of the position they are taking have yet to be worked out by the people involved.
The same demand for a fundamental constitutional revision has come from the other end of the chamber from spokesmen for the Ralliement Creditistes. No small or minor amendment is envisaged but rather a fundamental amendment which would give the same province, the province of Quebec, the equivalent status of associate state. Those who wish to see what are the implications of this might recall the constitution of Austro-Hungary before the first world war in order to find the closest parallel.
It is astonishing to me to see how many responsible people in this house, and outside it, men holding senior positions in the press and public life, are insisting that the constitution be blithely and fundamentally rewritten, and are ignoring the rule of unanimity of

the ten provinces, which has been scrupulously observed at the insistence of the province of Quebec. Has any one province the right to think that the rule of unanimity can be waived like this because that particular province wants to make a particular fundamental constitutional revision?
The great renaissance which is going on in Quebec fills us all with admiration. We are filled with respect for them when we read of the construction of the Manicouagan dams, the development of hydro resources and the tremendous effort they are putting into education. We know that the results of these efforts can only mean good for all of us. We know that in doing this the government of the province of Quebec is serving its people constructively and well. But there are those in the province of Quebec, the lunatic fringe- there is one in that province as well as in other places in Canada-who have built up a very different type of expectation, who have on occasion demonstrated that they would resort to terrorism and violence. But they are a small minority.
The question which comes to my mind is what will happen when the expectations which have been built up in the minds of this group for associate state status are not achieved. Let us be more specific. Suppose the parliament of the United Kingdom by 1967 or 1968 were faced with a resolution from one province asking for a fundamental constitutional revision. Suppose that one or two provinces also asked for relatively minor revisions, and also suppose that resolutions were presented from a large number, if not a majority, of the provinces opposing constitutional revision. Does anyone think the United Kingdom parliament would act in such circumstances? If the United Kingdom parliament did not choose to act in such circumstances, what would be the consequences to the expectations which some people are now building up?
I	suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these are reckless statements made by responsible people who should know better, and they are influencing certain people who are ready to do these things and think they are within the reach of realistic attainment. Will the disillusionment which will then take place take the form which a radical and dissident group in that province has shown on previous occasions?
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the present legislation goes just about as far as we can expect the federal government to go in meeting the requirements of provincial authori-
Federal-Provincial Relations ties for additional sources of revenue. We have in Canada very clear fields which are the responsibility of the provinces. There are equally fundamental responsibilities for national growth and development, areas which must be a federal responsibility. In between, Mr. Chairman, is an area where our co-operative federalism must work, where we must work together in this grey area to achieve federal-provincial co-operation in a constructive way to develop those services which we have the right to expect and which all Canadians hope we will achieve.

The new plan indicates that the additional amount that will be received by all the provinces in 1964-65 is $87,479 million; for 1965-66, $171,176 million, and for 196667, $264,973 million, or almost $265 million in round figures.
Sir, this is described as one of the greatest examples, if not the greatest, of the federal government translating the philosophy of cooperative federalism into practical dollars and cents. One naturally asks oneself this question. How is this extra amount of money to be raised? Is it going to be raised by added taxation on the part of a government that has already increased taxation in the period it has been in office by some $300 million a year? What is going to be done to meet even these additional amounts? Certainly there has been no indication given of the ways and means.

We used to hear arguments advanced in respect of the terrors of deficits, but the terrors of deficits are no longer felt by the government as they were when they were in opposition. The minister no longer talks of balanced budgets and no longer condemns deficits. Indeed, he embraces them to his bosom in a manner that is quite out of keeping with the views he expressed from 1961 on and, of course, even further removed from the views expressed in his one incursion into the book world.
Sir, I want to find out what is going to be done. How is this money going to be raised at the very time the United States of America, also with deficits, has greatly cut taxation? This government is increasing taxation and at the same time maintaining this very large deficit. I should like to know what the minister's philosophy is now. Does he believe that Canada can successfully compete for exports against the United States which under President Johnson has so materially reduced taxation? We want to know what the government's attitude is in respect of the problems of inflation.
During the period we were in office we maintained a level of prices in this country for the individual that was commended by the late president of the United States, President Kennedy, when he said that no other country in the western world had kept down the cost of living to the extent that Canada had. Today when the minister is asked these questions he just brushes them aside with generalities. The people in all parts of Canada are asking, what is his policy? What is being done to meet the increasing cost of living? What is being done to hold back the inflationary trend?

After all, surely Hansard is entitled to be wrong sometimes when the hon. gentleman regards $100 million as of such insignificance as he did just a few minutes ago. I will just place a summary of the figures for each province on the record, because it has been contended by the minister that this legislation is indeed the epitome of all the perfections in dominion-provincial relations. I should like to place on Hansard the figures in this regard for the last year of the St. Laurent government and the last year we were in office.
Starting with Prince Edward Island, the total amount paid to that province in 1956-57 was $5,048 million. I stated that I would also place on record the 1957-58 figures so no one could complain that I had disregarded the legislative enactments passed in the spring of 1957. The figure for 1957-58 was $7,072 million, while the figure for 1962-63 was $15,035 million or more than double the amount advanced in 1957-58.
For Nova Scotia the 1956-57 figure was $31,336 million while in 1957-58 it was $39,613 million and in 1962-63 $82,388 million. The increase was tremendous, more than double the amount available in 1957-58. For New Brunswick the amount in 1956-57 was $29,505 million, in 1957-58 $34,058 million and the preliminary estimate for 1962-63 was $66,484 million. There were vast increases in the case of the maritime provinces which had been neglected and starved for so long between 1935 and 1957.
I come now to Quebec. In 1956-57 the total amount by way of unconditional grants, conditional grants and payments for the benefit of provincial institutions was $177,463 million. In 1957-58 the amount was $205,896 million, while in 1962-63 it was $496,136 million, which represents a tremendous increase of approximately $250 million a year. Yet there are some who say that during the period we were in office we unjustly treated certain groups or provinces in this country.

For Ontario the figure in 1956-57 was $214.887 million. In 1957-58 it was $282,790 million and in 1962-63 the amount was $679,084 million. For Alberta the 1956-57 figure was $49,805 million, in 1957-58 $62,322 million and in 1962-63 $144,096 million. There is the same trend everywhere, vast increases of hundreds of millions of dollars and a total increase of over $1,000 million for all the provinces of Canada during the period we were in office. Yet those opposite speak of the increase being made under this present legislation as though it was something that had never taken place before. For British Columbia the 1956-57 figure was $77,911 million, in 1957-58 $92,690 million and in 1962-63 $159,096 million.
Those are the official figures, Mr. Chairman. Those are the figures that are appended as part of the record of the 1963 federal-provincial conference. Now, the minister has stated that there was some error in the record regarding the general, composite picture. If there was I can only say, as I said before, that Hansard had this particular document before it. If any correction is to be made I suggest that the minister do so, in order that all of us will fully understand what he meant by the interruption he just made while I was speaking.
There is the picture. It shows the tremendous increase in the assistance to the provinces to enable them to discharge their responsibilities. I repeat that if it had not been for our action in this regard we would not have had deficits during the period we were in office.
I come now to the question of the amounts that have been distributed. A moment ago I mentioned the promise made to the premier of Quebec. Whatever the amount was, it was certainly a long way removed from what actually has taken place. In the federal-provincial conference that took place in October, 1963 some $86 million was distributed. This distribution provided an extra amount for Newfoundland of $3,282 million; Prince Edward Island, $599,000; Nova Scotia, $5,742 million; New Brunswick, $5,558 million; Quebec, $42,716 million; Ontario, $14,416 million; Manitoba, $7,023 million; Saskatchewan, $2,469 million; Alberta, $1,722 million; British Columbia, $3,921 million. This division satisfied no one and was the reason for the major difficulties at the dominion-provincial conference early this year in Quebec city. What had happened was that consideration was promised, but consideration was given only to a modicum of what the promise actually was. I wanted to have the record clear so

there would be no misunderstanding of what has taken place under this legislation, because it represents very little compared to what was done on behalf of the provinces under the Conservative administration between 1957 and 1963.
When we come to those clauses dealing with the question of equalization, and the like, there will be some questions asked thereon. I am not going to say anything more at this time. One must be most careful not to raise any arguments in this house or continue the discussion of matters relating to hundreds of millions of dollars because there will be those who will say it is part of a plan to frustrate parliament. There was no better editorial on this subject than the one that appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune. I will not read it; I will simply bring it to the attention of the committee. It was entitled "Thermometer of Democracy". The title of itself is sufficient to indicate the purport of the argument advanced that there is a responsibility to discuss these matters, regardless of whether or not there be some who, either in their own interests or for political purposes, would endeavour to lead the people of Canada to believe that when arguments are made they are advanced for some improper purpose or, as some say, to bring about an election. This is furthest from our thoughts, and has been from the beginning. Our purpose is to discharge our responsibility, regardless of the thermometer, and to discharge it irrespective of the degree to which misrepresentations may be made as to our reasons.
If I may summarize, sir, I would say that after all the promises that were made as to what co-operative federalism would bring about, we find that the experience since April, 1963 can be properly interpreted by the phrase "muddled uncertainty." This has been a government of accidents. There have been constitutional accidents. So far as the minister is concerned, he has given paternity to a series of economic accidents. When one looks at what we have before us today I can only wonder what the Liberals sitting opposite would have said were they to describe it in the kind of terms they used when we were in office. Meaningless, they said; unimportant; merely a bone. We do not say that to them, although the minister does think $100 million is of no significance. But we do say that if the hon. member for Carleton, who is not in his seat now, was speaking with the authority that his appearance would indicate, it is a sad day for the provinces of Canada;

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I do not have very much to say at this stage of this debate. I have already expressed some opinions during the resolution stage, and if I rise at all at this moment it is to continue along the line which the Leader of the Opposition has just taken with regard to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Carleton.
I know he is a private member, as he so modestly and humbly stated to all of us, and we believe that to be the case. At the same time we know-and I do not think his modesty will be shocked when I say this- that he is a much respected supporter of the present parliament and, whether or not he speaks with the tacit or explicit approval of the Minister of Finance or other front benchers, his words cannot fail to find an echo in their minds and be reflected in the decisions they may make in the future.
The hon. member for Carleton brought out a number of interesting points, and I listened to them with great attention. First, in regard to co-operative federalism, he seems to think that anyone who criticizes this approach is almost a traitor to this country; that is the only way in which I can interpret some of his remarks. Well, I think co-operative federalism has been a complete failure, no matter how many smokescreens the government may put up to disguise the real position. I believe it has been a failure not only from the point of view of the province I happen to represent but also from the point of view of the other provinces. Many enlightened people in Canada are asking, is it co-operation? Is it even

Federal-Provincial Relations federalism? I, for one, have great doubts that it is federalism.
What are the objections to co-operative federalism? Some people say-this is the thesis of many authoritative spokesmen of the province of Quebec-that it is a disguised way of violating the constitution. This is what it amounts to; because apparently it is held by those who advocate cooperative federalism that the provinces can agree together and, by agreement reached behind closed doors, arrive at decisions which are plainly contrary to the provisions of the British North America Act.
I know the hon. member for Carleton may say "What does it matter, provided we agree?" But we cannot, by agreement, commit a crime or perform any other illicit action. Similarly, those who from time to time represent provinces cannot by agreement bind their provinces for the future when it is contrary to the law of the land. Yet that is what they are doing, and this is why so many people have drawn attention to the dangers that are inherent in this approach to co-operative federalism. These are serious objections raised by people who are constitutional authorities in the province of Quebec, objections made in good faith by people who are in favour of co-operation and in favour of confederation.
Where is this approach likely to lead us? Many people believe that, perhaps unconsciously and in an indirect way, the government is leading up to a situation which amounts to de facto separatism. Many editorials in publications throughout Canada have raised this question, and the government has not been able to answer. The situation now is that the federal government, for alleged reasons of economic necessity or for other reasons, is invading those fields which the hon. member for Carleton called "grey fields", though I do not think they are grey at all; to me they are either black or white. In any event the federal government says to the provinces, referring particularly, perhaps, to the province of Quebec, "You have nothing to worry about because you can opt out if you wish to do so". A provincial government which finds itself unable to accept the proposition then signifies to the central government its intention to opt out and, in compensation, receives a fiscal concession of some sort so that it may go ahead and implement its own plan. After this process has been repeated over and over again in various fields one ends up with a situation which amounts to de facto separatism, a situation
tMr. Martlneau.]
where there is one law for one part of the country and another for the rest.
I say there are serious and well founded objections to this approach along the lines of co-operative federalism. I say it is not a solution. It is not a solution for those who believe in a strong central government, and it is not a solution for those-and I am one of them-who while being convinced federalists and admirers of confederation stand for the rights of the provinces. The way to go about this is surely to bring the various parties together and seek an amendment to the constitution itself. Then if there are departures from the present way of doing things, those departures will be based on a legal enactment. At this time there is no legal basis for the way in which the government is carrying on its relations with the provinces, fiscal or otherwise. That is why I protest.
The hon. member for Carleton says those who argue in favour of constitutional amendment, or repatriation of the constitution, do not know what they are talking about. I can only say he is placing the Prime Minister of this land in that very position, because the right hon. gentleman has made numerous speeches in this house pointing out the need to effect the changes necessary to bring about that harmony which is essential to the very future of this country. That is the logical approach to this question. We cannot bury our heads in the sand like ostriches. We cannot be content to say that as long as we are able to reach agreement we shall pursue our objectives, and if Quebec or some other province does not like it, they can opt out.
Mr. Chairman, it does not take too much imagination to see where that can lead. The hon. member for Carleton said "You cannot get a constitutional amendment, because you cannot get agreement". He said that the last time an attempt was made the province of Quebec, for very good reasons, refused to accept the formula. As I recall, it was not the province of Quebec at all that refused to accept the formula for this repatriation; it was the province of Saskatchewan. They were the nigger in the woodpile in that particular instance.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member wants to quote me he should quote me correctly. He has misquoted me twice in the last minute. One misquotation was when the hon. member said I had said people did not know what they were talking about. I never used that language. The second was, with regard to the last attempt to amend the constitution I did

not say that any particular province was the objector; I did not name any particular province in that connection.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can with difficulty quote the hon. member, because I do not have his text. But I did listen to him very carefully. I do not pretend to quote him, but I do think I am commenting in a fair way on his remarks. I am not going to quote him word for word; I do not want to, and he cannot force me to do so. But I think his words are open to fair comment in this house, and they will be as far as I am concerned.
The hon. member went on to say "Well, you cannot have it both ways". I agree that you cannot have it both ways; but you certainly can, if you are conscious of a malaise, which is very apparent in this country in the relations between the federal government and the provinces, and indeed a malaise in the very fibre of confederation, try to find ways and means of seeking out that malaise and eliminating it. The way to do it is certainly by a constitutional convention or, if you like, a constituent assembly; call it whatever you will, but in any case an assembly where the federal and provincial authorities and those concerned with the problem can meet and consult.
I know the objection to that is "Well, you cannot get agreement among the participants". That is obviously a very negative approach. On July 13 I spoke on this resolution and I approved of the idea, submitted by the Leader of the Opposition, of a constitutional meeting. I went further and said I thought it should be a constituent assembly. But I also said that preparations for that meeting should be made long in advance by a series of meetings at the provincial level; a meeting of specialists; by setting up a constitutional committee of the Senate and House of Commons, and by all these bodies and people getting together and preparing an agenda upon which the participants could be reasonably expected to agree. When that has been done and the assembly does take place, I have reason to believe that if we do not solve all the problems which beset confederation at least we will have made a very good start.
That is simply the attitude that we on this side of the house have taken all along. I have stated time after time that I felt confederation was a success, but that it must be improved; and the urgency to improve it is all the greater when one considers the renaissance of Quebec to which the hon. member for Carleton referred a few minutes ago.
Federal-Provincial Relations
The province of Quebec, today more than ever before, is conscious of its power and weight within confederation, and is anxious to play its full part within confederation. It is seeking ways and means whereby it can preserve its identity and at the same time progress with the rest of Canada. If thinking in such a way is being reactionary or is a threat to confederation, I am guilty of that offence, Mr. Chairman.
These are the terms in which I have always spoken. I have time and time again condemned, for instance, the attitude taken by the group on my extreme left, which attitude was again brought out by the meeting last week end in Quebec city. That group has come out very squarely for the status of an associate state and has asked that the future associate state, if it is the province of Quebec, have full control of credit, of immigration, of imports and exports. They say Quebec should also be fully responsible for the collection of its taxes.
I think if such an attitude is adopted it is simply and purely separatism, and nothing else. Whether or not they use the term, it can only lead to separatism. How can a province or a state, if you want to call it a state, be a member of a federation when at the same time the central government that speaks for the federation cannot collect any taxes for that province? There is no representation without taxation; therefore if the future associate state, that exists only in the imagination of a few on the extreme left of the chamber, is to come about you will have separatism.
I therefore condemn the attitude that was taken by the Ralliement because it is a completely hypocritical attitude. If they adopt attitudes that are separatist let them say they are separatist and they will be more respected for it. But even while adopting that attitude they are afraid to say outright that their attitude can lead to nothing but separatism.
I have heard the hon. member for Lapointe and others point out the condition of the state or colony, whatever it may be, of Puerto Rico and say that is the form of government toward which the province of Quebec should evolve. That is utter and complete nonsense, and no one in his right mind can take any other attitude in that regard. The state of Puerto Rico does not have the right to elect anyone to the United States congress. It is not represented there; it does not pay taxes, and has nothing to say about the way in which the United States is administered. It may have some local authority, but that is all.

Federal-Provincial Relations That is not the future I envisage for my province, and it is not the future I envisage for Canada as a whole.
I think the attitude of the Ralliement is not only hypocritical but is also opportunist, because its members were elected on a monetary reform ticket. The people who voted for these members did so in good faith, thinking they were backing a federal party which had some chance, as it seemed at that time, if not to attain power at least to have a substantial say in the balance of power and also to bring into effect the monetary reforms which it preached. But it broke up; the party split up into two wings and the Ralliement, seeing that no one in the province of Quebec or elsewhere would take it seriously on its platform of monetary reform, has now swerved sharply toward an extremist and separatist attitude for which it has no mandate and which certainly the bulk of the population in the province of Quebec will not follow. It has not studied the implications of that position and it has not got the capacity or the knowledge to implement it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow a question?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member has just stated that the monetary reform proposed by the Social Crediters cannot be accepted by anybody. Does he mean by that that the 600,000 French Canadians who voted for Social Credit are all insane?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is clear that the hon. member misunderstood the meaning of my remarks, because I said indeed that those who voted for Social Credit in the last general election were of good faith and sincerely believed that the Social Crediters who would be elected would endeavour to apply the monetary reform they had preached throughout the province. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue stated that we were not of good faith and that we did not apply our monetary doctrine. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member's question of privilege is ill-founded and rather tends to start a debate.
I have certain opinions concerning the approach and the program of the Ralliement Creditiste and I am entitled to put them forward. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question? Would he tell the house whether he makes a distinction between the Social Crediters who are extremist nationalists and those who are not?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is clear that I must make a distinction, because I am referring to the Creditiste convention held in Quebec and called together by the Ralliement Creditiste, and the supporters of that group have nothing to do with those who support the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson).
The members of the Ralliement Creditiste are not qualified to give leadership to the province of Quebec or to the Canadian confederation, and in adopting such an opportunist stand, they are now trying to use the cloak of nationalism to come into office either at the federal or at the provincial level.
Mr. Chairman, I think that responsible people in the province of Quebec will condemn such an attitude and will realize that they are merely dealing with opportunists.
I suggest that they should think of what is happening in the world at this time, and more particularly of the pan-African conference held at Cairo last week, or of the gigantic efforts being made in favour of the unification of Europe.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not feel the hon. member should be allowed to refer to the Ralliement Creditiste convention when we are dealing with fiscal arrangements between the federal government and the provinces. I therefore ask you to call the hon. member to order.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I believe this bill passed through a resolution stage, at which time there was a general debate. I believe the bill had a second reading stage, where there was a general debate. I believe we are now in committee on

the first clause of the bill. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I speak to the point of order. As the hon. member for Port Arthur has said, the debate has been broad and it would not be fair to curtail it. However, my remarks are directly related to the bill because they concern fiscal relations between the provinces and the federal government. I have spoken about co-operative federalism; I have also spoken against an attitude which is very topical and which was adopted last Sunday at Quebec city. If that attitude were to prevail it would make a mockery of the present bill, which tends to regulate fiscal relations between the central government and the provinces. That is the reason I am bringing that out at this stage, and I do so for no other reason.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I will certainly do that, Mr. Chairman, although I think I have been confining myself rather closely to the implications of clause 1. If attitudes such as those which have been adopted by the members of the Ralliement were to prevail we would have to vote against the bill. According to these people there would be no fiscal arrangements possible at all, because if you follow their theory the imaginary associate state of the future would not be subject to taxation. That is the reason it is so pertinent to
Federal-Provincial Relations the bill to bring out what I think are false theories concerning federal-provincial relations. However, I shall abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and bring these few remarks to a speedy conclusion.
I was just telling hon. members of the Ralliement that their attitude is reactionary in view of the trends throughout the world and in view of the real needs of our own country. As I said at the start, and I will say again, I believe that Canada by and large has been a happy and prosperous country under confederation, and it behooves us to try to conserve and preserve that system. But it will only be conserved and preserved, and it can only survive, if we become fully conscious of the problems which are besetting confederation, and if we have the will to solve them. And we will have the will to solve them, Mr. Chairman, if we simply recognize the basic fact of Canadian life-call it the French fact, call it the English fact, call it Quebec, call it whatever you like-the aspiration of the people of the province of Quebec to fulfil their destiny and play their full part within our nation.
Mr. Chairman, I will challenge any member of this house to attend a forum anywhere in Canada and debate that question. I send this challenge particularly to the member for Carleton who seems to come to wrong conclusions about remarks that may be made in this house. If he or anyone else is sincerely animated with a desire to make things better and more acceptable, let them participate in such a debate.
I will combat any reactionary attitude taken by the Ralliement. I will also combat the hypocritical attitude taken by the present government, as indicated by its highfalutin phrases such as "co-operative federalism". I have never heard the present government, and least of all the Minister of Finance, define what he means by co-operative federalism. He does not seem to know what it means. Every time the members of the government are invited to speak to different bodies in various provinces of the country they do so in flowing terms about this new era of cooperative federalism. To my mind their policy is neither co-operative nor federalism.
The answer to present problems is not contained in the proposals of the Ralliement. The answer is not contained in the present attitude of the government in shying away from its responsibilities in this regard. The answer lies in a statement admitting that the problem exists, and an honest endeavour to find a

Federal-Provincial Relations solution. The Prime Minister has had the courage on more than one occasion to admit that there is a problem. I applauded him on those occasions and will applaud him again. Unfortunately he has not had the determination to deal effectively with this problem. That is why we accuse the present government of a lack of determination.
The step to be taken and the course to be followed is contained in the proposals we have made in respect of constitutional assembly preceded by all the safeguards I have enumerated on previous occasions. I urge this committee to seek this solution in a broad spirit of true confederation and co-operation. If the government gives a lead we on this side will follow enthusiastically. We believe in the future of our country which we all love.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS

Mr. Chairman, the answer
should be obvious, even to the hon. member.

Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Additional grant to Newfoundland.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in view of the importance of clause 3 to my province of Newfoundland, may I ask the minister whether clause 3 has been designed after careful consideration of term 29 of the terms of union of Canada with Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did intend to make a remark in respect of clause 3 to clarify that point.
Clause 3 under the heading, Newfoundland grant, was inserted in this bill because the bill itself was amending the Federal-Frovin-


cial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, and it was felt that advantage should be taken of this fact to remove the limitation on these payments in that act to March 31, 1967.
While in opposition the present Prime Minister gave the following undertaking:
A new Liberal government will restore term 29 to the constitution, and ask the parliament of Canada to guarantee the payments to Newfoundland under term 29 so long as they are not changed by an agreement freely made between the government of Newfoundland and Canada. A Liberal government in Canada made the agreement with Newfoundland and a Liberal government will see the agreement is kept in letter and in spirit.
Neither the Prime Minister nor the government regards the present amendment as a full discharge of this undertaking. It is the intention of the government, during the life of the present parliament, to bring in a separate measure which will carry out that undertaking and which will relate it to the terms of union with Newfoundland, of which it is essentially a part.
It was however thought that since the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act had to be amended at this time anyway, the limitation as to date should be taken out at once pending the more formal step which must be taken in order to recognize the constitutional right of Newfoundland as embodied in term 29 of the terms of union.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-Change in computation of "standard individual income tax".

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of this House of Commons from the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario I presume many think I should approach with diffidence any discussion of the fiscal tax sharing arrangements with the provinces. I wish to comment on the method of computing the tax moneys which are allocated to eight of the ten provinces, and I do so in all sincerity because I love this country of ours.
I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and the hon. member for Toronto-Davenport, both of whom expressed themselves on Friday, that the confederation will remain and become stronger and greater in the future. I do not believe that confederation will fall apart. I believe that only by careful examination of the fiscal arrangements between the ten provinces and the federal government can we maintain that equanimity of feeling which is much to be desired, particularly if we are to accomplish the building of this nation into a stronger and greater Canada.

I am sure we are all familiar with the proverb: The squeaky wheel gets the most grease. It would appear that some individuals are aware of that proverb. I would remind them of another: Still waters run deep. We have heard a great deal of comment and complaint about the feelings of one province being different from those of the other nine. Some people take every opportunity to unburden their mouths of any weight they may feel on their tongues.
I should like to point out that the people of my riding are not the only people in Canada who feel the formula on which these tax-sharing arrangements are based needs to be carefully scrutinized and rewritten. You have heard the hon. member for Carleton express himself today to the effect that the federal government has gone as far as it can go in respect of these tax-sharing arrangements without weakening the central authority. I should like to point out that I believe in equalization payments. I believe it is necessary for a strong central government to make sure that those areas of this nation, which do not have fiscal resources upon which they can draw to make them as strong as the strongest parts, do receive help. I do not believe that the strong and able sections of this country are entitled to fiscal payment. They are well able to look after themselves.
I would mention two episodes that occurred in Toronto. Many years ago there was a great drive to build a community hall, skating rink and gathering place in north Toronto. Thousands of people put their hearts and souls into the drive and a great deal of money was raised before the campaign was halted by the realization that the money was not reaching the end to which it had been directed by the donors. There was quite a bit of talk and comment. The drive came to a sudden stop and it took some years before the people of north Toronto recovered sufficiently to build on a smaller scale. But they are still conscious of the fact that money voluntarily given did not achieve the purpose intended because of the hands through which it passed.
Then we had the sad experience in my own riding of York-Humber of hurricane Hazel in 1954 when a great deal of damage was done and 74 lives were lost by drowning. There was a tremendous upsurge of public opinion in favour of helping those who needed help and great contributions were made. Large sums of money were raised. But is was suddenly found that a great deal of the money 20220-422
Federal-Provincial Relations was not reaching the end for which it was intended and a great freeze developed among the goodhearted people who felt the victims of hurricane Hazel should be helped. They wanted to help them but they felt that as long as there was a toll gate between them and the victims of hurricane Hazel they would allow their wellsprings of charity to dry up.
So far as fiscal arrangements are concerned I am all for aiding those areas that definitely need help, and when I state I am in favour of a change in the formula I am only repeating statements made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Medicine Hat. They emphasized that the factors being used in devising the formula for the payment of these moneys needed to be drastically overhauled. As a private member I should like to state that I agree with the comments made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for Medicine Hat in their thoughtful and thought provoking comments with regard to the manner in which provinces are judged to be wealthy and well able to extend assistance to others.
When the hon. member for Burnaby-Co-quitlam was speaking he made such statements as "I criticize the formula", "I think there are many things wrong with the formula", "there must be some pooling and some sharing of the tax revenues, particularly tax revenues which are jointly occupied by the federal and provincial governments, namely, income, corporation and inheritance taxes". So many comments were made with regard to the formula and the way in which it was devised that the Minister of Finance, who has my unbounded admiration and to whom I give 100 per cent allegiance in the difficult task he has before him, when commenting on August 7 on what the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam had said, made this statement, as found on page 6651 of Hansard:
The difficulty is to find a formula with which everybody will agree. I am not prepared for a minute to say that the formulae developed in the past were perfect or that they could not be improved on. I am not prepared to say that the present formula cannot be improved upon...There are many other difficulties.. .which are contained in this formula. I do not think it is perfect. I am not pretending that it is or pretending to defend it in that respect.
I think that was spoken like a man who is faced with the problem of province after province demanding more and more money, and the hon. member for Davenport is the man who is supposed to be able to produce it.

Federal-Provincial Relations I say to hon. members that there is a limit to which the Minister of Finance can go, and the hon. member for Carleton has stated definitely that he thinks that limit has been reached. There are a few of us who think that the limit has been exceeded.
We are told that the only way we can have unity in this country is to assist the provinces in their aspirations. That is a great phrase-assist them in their aspirations. It is softer than "yield to their demands". I would point out that when children ask their father for something he has to determine his gifts to his young ones on his ability to supply them. Just because children ask and ask and ask for more and more and more is no reason for thinking that the father is able to supply, supply, supply. In answer to such demands the father tells his children: I am unable to meet your desires in that regard but I will do my best. If I cannot give you a Thunder-bird car as your own personal possession we will allow you to ride in the family car. If we cannot give you seven changes of raiment, one for each day in the week, we will at least keep the one or two suits you have in good repair.
Surely to heaven the federal government, surely to heaven the Minister of Finance- I say this without having spoken to him in advance-are entitled to say:	Curb your
aspirations, curb your requests; there is a limit to what can be done and it looks to many of us as though that limit had been reached.
The hon. member for Carleton made a direct reference to the province of Quebec. I am happy he made that reference because if I had been the first to make a direct reference to Quebec the newspapers would immediately have headlined me as a hater of Quebec, a hater of French Canadians, a hater of everything east of the Ottawa river. In the name of God, I do not know anybody in this house who is more favourably disposed to the province of Quebec than I am. My mother and father are still living at Messines 90 miles up the Gatineau. I have a married brother in Montreal. My oldest married daughter is living in Quebec city and raising four children there. I have cousins throughout the province and I have known it all my life.
When I speak about Quebec I am confining myself to factual matters because some people who endeavour to speak for the province cause a lot of umbrage in certain quarters by statements they make which cannot be founded on fact. I have here the debates of

the House of Commons for the 1963 session, volume I, May and June, 1963. I refer to pages 152 and 153 where a speech by the hon. member for lies-de-la-Madeleine is to be found. He was speaking about how hard done by his native province is and I quote him as follows:
I have before me a document which shows that there was $497 difference in 1961 in the personal income as between a resident of Ontario and a resident of Quebec; this means that in Ontario the per capita income was $1,829 while in the province of Quebec it was only $1,382, a difference of 37 per cent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, how can the citizens of the province of Quebec...be willing to accept a situation where they are at a financial disadvantage compared to the citizens of Ontario?
He went on to say:
-unless the central government.. .comes and facilitates the renovation work undertaken by the Liberal government of Quebec... Quebec shall not be able to achieve the aims which we have set forth and consequently, we shall continue to have grievances against the rest of Canada.
He did not identify the document from which he read. I have before me the document which shows a difference of $497 in 1961 between the per capita income of residents of Ontario and Quebec. The words he used were "as between a resident of Ontario and a resident of Quebec". This is the difference in the per capita income. Why this table appears in the national accounts, income and expenditures booklet put out by the dominion bureau of statistics, I will never know.
This book, under table 29 for the year 1961, shows the per capita income for Quebec is $1,382; the per capita income for Ontario is $1,829 or a difference of 37 per cent. But I ask you, why in the name of heaven should every baby at the breast, child in his cot or kid in his crib be counted in considering income of a province and a demand be made that every one of them have the same per capita income as the other provinces where the number of children is not so large?
Let me give you figures to show the position of the province of Quebec. It is not 37 per cent inferior to the province of Ontario. I have in my hand the taxation statistics published by the Department of National Revenue for the year 1961. They show you that the number of taxable returns from Quebec in 1961 was 1,122,096. The total income assessed was $4,790,503,000. The average income per taxpayer-not the number of children nor the number of babies-the average income per taxpayer in Quebec was $4,269. In Ontario, the number of taxable returns for the same year was 1,886,702. The

total income assessed was $8,486,573,000. The average income per taxpayer was $4,498. The average income in Ontario was $4,498 per taxpayer and in Quebec it was $4,269. This is a distinction of only 5.3 per cent and is a great deal different from this per capita of 37 per cent, which signifies nothing.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext: May I ask a question? Does that include those who do not earn enough to pay income tax?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I point out that the figures are available from the taxation statistics of the Department of National Revenue to indicate the number of people who file income tax returns but do not pay income tax because of the amount of their exemptions. These figures indicate that the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec compare very well. I went down to the Department of National Revenue and asked them about these figures for people who do not pay any income tax and who are listed in the green book. I was advised that the Department of National Revenue is very happy with the returns they are receiving from the people of Canada, those who have to pay income tax and those who do not. They advised me that many of the returns from those who do not pay income tax are sent in by people who wish to obtain refunds of income tax deducted at the source. In looking at the population statistics published by the dominion bureau of statistics, the Department of National Revenue feels that the figures shown for non-taxpaying people are quite accurate. If there is anyone who wishes to look at the taxation statistics booklet he can find the figures indicating the number of people who do not pay any income tax in any of the ten provinces. He will be interested in seeing that on an average basis Ontario and Quebec are nearly equal.

I have in my hand a Canadian Press dispatch sent out of Ottawa from the press gallery here on Friday of last week. It deals with the bill we are now considering and one of the sentences in this dispatch which went to every daily newspaper and every radio and television station in Canada, reads:

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who is now speaking -and I enjoy hearing the results of the research he has carried out on this matter- continually refers to "eight provinces".
