maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROVISION FOR REVISION OF FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND TAXATION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the comment of the hon. member. I spoke to the Department of Finance on this very point this morning and said it looked to me, from the working papers they had given me, that three provinces would not share in these payments. I was advised that in regard to some of the payments in these years there would be three provinces not participating, but for most of the years there would only be two because of this natural resources formula doing its bit of work.
I was referring to the fact that Burke at one time said there is a limit at which forbearance ceases to be a virtue, and frankly I think our forbearance has gone far enough in this regard. I would like to give the committee the example of how the per capita angle under clause 4 can affect the payments made under the equalization formula. I trust the committee will follow me carefully when I point out that in the province of Quebec 44.3 per cent of the population is of the age of 18 years and under. It can be said that those of 18 years of age and under are the least productive of the entire population; but when you start to roll in 44.3 per cent of the population on a per capita basis, you certainly play hob with the figures.
I would point out that if you have a large number of children, when you come to make your income tax return the tax payable is very much reduced. There are many, many people who are exempt from paying income tax because of the simple fact that their exemptions remove them from the tax bracket and they are therefore not liable for tax. The little ones help them to avoid paying income tax. In this connection we can compare Ontario with Quebec, for the purposes of have and have-not ratios, on the basis of income tax receipts. If you do not pay in-

come tax because of the number of children you have, the youngsters are helping you in keeping the base down for that province. In another province, where you do not have so many children per family, you are paying income tax. That is considered a sign of wealth. Then you have the youngsters coming along and drawing the family bonus allowance, as it is called, or the family assistance allowance; and the more of them there are, the larger are the payments to the individual families. Then for the third time the children are trotted in, and we are told that on a per capita basis the wealth of Quebec is considerably less than that of other provinces. They use their children to avoid considerable income tax payments, because the exemptions for children remove the parents from the income tax rolls. The number of children increases the gap that appears to exist between the provinces when one looks at the income tax returns and the amount of tax collected. They draw more money because of the family assistance program which this Liberal government initiated, and which I support 100 per cent, and then they trot the children out the fourth time to prove that on a per capita basis the income is not as great as that of other provinces. It almost makes me think that the children are being used as apprentices of mammon.
I would point out that on the largesse that is being distributed to the eight provinces on the basis of equalization, we are bringing eight provinces to the level of two. This is not the equalization basis that has been used for the past several years. On that basis the provinces were brought up to the national level; but by altering the regulations we are adding $55 million in the year 1964-65 to the equalization payments because we are raising the equalization payments to the level of the top two provinces, instead of their being brought to the national level, which system has been in effect for the last several years. Of the $55,309,000 that will be added to the equalization payments this year, 61 per cent of the increase, or $34,130,000, goes to the province of Quebec. Next year, of course, there will be another increase, and in 1966-67 there will be the biggest increase of all, whereby the province of Quebec will draw 61 per cent of the increase between the years 1965 and 1966, and 1966 and 1967. I make the statement that this is going altogether too far. Surely we can tell this province, "We cannot pass out this kind of money. There is a limit to what the taxpayers of this country

can pay out". We must use reason and good sense in this matter.
Why do we pick the natural resources
revenues of the provinces as an indication of wealth? There are oil wells in Alberta and there are forests in British Columbia, and they have a lot of these natural resources. The way they collect the revenue from them sets them apart. If the formula read that all provinces bordering on the Saguenay river would be considered as have-not provinces, and all other provinces would be considered as have provinces, you would say things were a little too blunt. So now we have the natural resources revenue-not the natural resources. Does anybody think the natural resources of British Columbia are any greater than the natural resources of Quebec? Look at the aluminum development in the Saguenay; look at the pulp and paper development, the asbestos, the base metal mining, the gold mining developments there are in the province of Quebec. It is not the value of the natural resources that is considered in the formula; it is the amount of tax money received by the province from the natural resources.
If one province determines to tax in one way, and another province determines to tax in another, I see no reason why two provinces should be penalized in the federal held because of the manner in which they collect taxes from their natural resources. I would ask most sincerely that a change be made in this formula, and soon. A fairly good way to judge the wealth of a province was suggested the other day by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. He suggested that gasoline tax revenues would be indicative of the wealth of a province. I believe he also suggested that the revenue from liquor taxes would be a good indication of the wealth of a province, or the retail sales taxes collected in a province would be a good indication of the wealth of that province. I agree 100 per cent. Why not consider the donations made to charitable causes as an indication of the wealth of a province? In the province of Quebec, in 1962 the donations to charitable causes, as shown on income tax returns, amounted to $157 million. In the province of Ontario from which I come, the donations to charitable causes amounted to $84,560,000. What does that denote? Does it denote a have-not province, when one donates $157 million and the other $84 million? In 1962 Ontario's charitable donations amounted to .94 per cent of total income. Quebec donated 3.07 per cent of total income. You will be interested to know, Mr. Federal-Provincial Relations Chairman, that for the year 1961 Quebec donated $164,616,000 to charity and the rest of Canada donated $137,713,000. Why cannot we take that as one of the indicia of wealth?
I say to this committee that this formula needs to be worked over fast and worked over seriously. This bill which we are being asked to pass will be law for three years, unless it is amended. Therefore I suggest that it should be amended. We are now in committee stage following second reading. The proposition has been before the country for some years, but I believe the public will understand a little more how the formula is worked out from the facts and figures I have given, as well as the facts and figures put on the record by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the statement made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson and the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton, as well as the statement of the Minister of Finance who does not consider the formula perfect. I say this formula should be worked over right away. I can see no connection whatsoever between the fertility of the forests, fields of oil, the farms and factories of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario and the fervent fecundity of Quebec.

At this time, surveys are being made in the Gaspe peninsula under the ARDA program. Why? Precisely in order to give some assistance to people who are literally starving because they have not been sufficiently helped in the past.
At present ARDA is used not only in Quebec, but in other provinces, to reorganize rural establishments or to set up a new secondary industry, to help those people who at this time are neither being fairly treated nor able to make a decent living.
Mr. Chairman, the bill now before us is a first step, but it is not enough.
The matter of estates is strictly under provincial jurisdiction. Indeed, I have here before me statements made by the various provincial premiers during the federal-provincial conference of November 25, 1963. Let us for instance take the statement of Mr. Jean Lesage, premier of the province of Quebec, who said:
Since the beginning of confederation, it has been recognized that Quebec always firmly demanded respect of its jurisdiction.
That is all we claim.
With regard to tax sharing, Mr. Lesage stated:	'
Our chief and most urgent reason for demanding a new tax distribution plan at this time is the priority of provincial needs.
The purpose of tax sharing is to meet those requirements, that is to enable the provinces to dedicate themselves more fully and more efficiently to the development, if we may say so, of their human capital.
That is all we are asking for. Quebec does not need the hon. member for York-Humber for its development. Quebec can do it by 

itself providing it is given the tools. That is what is lacking.
Mr. Chairman, was it not on April 5, 1963, that Mr. Lesage stated:
In terms of fiscal powers, we are asking for 25 per cent of personal income tax, 25 per cent of corporation income taxes-in the latter case, that is about 10J per cent of the taxable income -and 100 per cent of succession duties because real estate transfers come under provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Chairman, those taxation rights which were granted to the federal government during the war were only loaned; they were not granted forever; after the war, the federal government was to give back to the provinces their taxation rights in the field of personal and corporate income taxes.
Mr. Chairman, under this bill and more particularly under section 40, Mr. Lesage will get about 50 per cent of his requests.
I also have here a statement made by Mr. Louis J. Robichaud, premier of New Brunswick, at that same federal-provincial conference.
The government of New Brunswick never willingly accepted-
That is the statement of a Liberal provincial government.
The government of New Brunswick never willingly accepted the terms of fiscal arrangements entered into by the provinces and the federal government.
Those agreements were a step backward, and one of major importance, in the efforts being made to recognize the differences in economic level among the various provinces.
Mr. Chairman, here we have a small province, New Brunswick, recognizing as justified the claims put forth by the premier of the province of Quebec, as well as those made by the premier of British Columbia at the same federal-provincial conference.
Mr. Chairman, I do not hesitate for a moment to state at this time that the kind of comments uttered a while ago by the hon. member for York-Humber constitutes the best separatist speech I have ever heard in my life, even in the province of Quebec. We have our separatists in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, but we also have others in Ontario, as I have pointed out in the past.
At the same federal-provincial conference, the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Bennett, stated:

The constitution, however, not only dictated the service responsibilities of the provincial legislatures, but to finance the necessary costs it also specified their taxation rights. One of these rghts, designated as an "exclusive power", was the use of direct taxation within the province.

The government of British Columbia is requesting exactly the same thing as the Quebec premier.
The premier of British Columbia also had this to say:

Sole provincial use of income taxes was respected by the federal government for 50 years preceding world war I. Federal entry in 1917 was explained as a temporary action in a time of national emergency. Recognition of provincial direct taxation rights was confirmed by Sir Thomas White, then federal minister of finance, who stated:
"The income tax is peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the province and is a suitable tax for the purpose of the province. .. .1 have placed no time limit upon this taxation measure; but I do suggest, and I should like this suggestion to be on Hansard, that after the war is over this taxation measure should be deliberately reviewed."

Mr. Chairman, those are the various points discussed by the premiers at the federal-provincial conference of November 1963.
We of the Ralliement Creditiste have made a stand last year for the suggestion or claims of the premier of Quebec to the effect that the personal and corporate income taxes belong to the provinces.
Moreover, as I said a while ago, succession duties come under the civil code and belong to the provinces. The priority needs of the provinces are especially felt in the fields of education, health, highways, the development of natural resources and the establishment of secondary industries. The provinces must have the financial means to do that, and the federal government is unable at the present time to give them those means.
On several occasions, we suggested that the central government should instruct the Bank of Canada to make available to the provinces the credits required for their economic development, their political organization if you wish, but especially for the satisfaction of the needs of consumers in each province. speechtext:
Clause 4 in this bill which is now before us, Mr. Chairman, is really the operative clause of the bill because it sets forth the formula upon which financial assistance to the provinces is to be based. I am not going to thresh old straw by going over the arguments with reference to our criticism of this formula. However I must say that the minister's explanation of a few moments ago seemed to me to be a lame excuse. He said it was difficult to have a conference agree on a formula and that this was something which took a great deal of time. He said that it could not be done quickly. I should like to point out to the committee that we had a very good equalization formula and that, in the main, it was satisfactory except that there were many who felt it should be equalized to the top province. The Liberal party agreed with this suggestion because they put it in their program and pledged themselves to do this. Apart from that provision, the rest of the formula was eminently satisfactory.
If the government was prepared to give more money to the provinces, they had before them the very simple expedient of increasing the abatement on income tax payments, corporation tax payments and succession duty payments to the provinces. This would have increased the amount of money which the provinces would have received but it would have continued to distribute that additional amount of money on the same equalization basis which obtained heretofore, with the exception of course of equalizing to the top province.
Anyone who examines the new formula will certainly see it is not an improvement, except with regard to equalizing to the top two provinces. One cannot escape the conclusion, no matter how kindly disposed he might be, that the extraneous factors which have been
[Mr. CaouetteJ

introduced into this formula were introduced with a calculated end in view. The Minister of Forestry, when he was reprimanding the hon. member for York-Humber, reminded him he was committed to the Liberal program of equalization. It is quite true that the Liberal party is pledged to a program of equalization. Liberal literature entitled, "The Liberals Have the Answer; the Pearson Plan," contains a paragraph indicating that the provinces should receive equal revenue per head of population of the tax fields shared between the two levels of government so that all Canadians will benefit equally. The Prime Minister, speaking in the House of Commons on June 2, 1958, as recorded at page 733 of Hansard said:
So far as this party are concerned, we are pledged to equalization on the basis of the per capita yield of the three taxes in the wealthiest province.
The Liberal party is clearly on record as favouring the principle of equalization on the basis of the three shared tax fields and the factors which are now being introduced into the formula are a departure from equalization. They represent a reversal of policy. We are now departing from the equalization principle. I hope that before this clause is passed the minister will give us some further explanation with reference to two of these very fundamental changes. The first is the introduction as a factor in determining equalization payments, the revenue which a province receives from resource development.
As the minister himself pointed out, as recorded at page 5182 of Hansard, the revenue which provinces get from resources is quite varied. As he pointed out, it varies all the way from 15 cents per capita in Prince Edward Island to a high of $94.08 per capita in Alberta. As the hon. member for York-Humber pointed out, resources and resource revenue are two entirely different things. When you look at the provinces of Quebec and Ontario you find that the per capita resource revenue in the case of Quebec is $6.62 and in the case of Ontario, $6.92 as compared with British Columbia where the per capita revenue is $37.72. I am sure no person would argue that the province of British Columbia has five or six times as much resources as either Ontario or Quebec. The fact is that the revenue varies as between these different provinces because some of the older provinces in days gone by disposed of their resources, in some cases for large sums of money. They have already sold some of their capital, and having disposed of their capital they do not receive revenue from

it. The selection, therefore, of this factor in determining equalization payments was the selection of one of the most unfair factors that could possibly have been chosen.
If the government was going to take the revenues of the provinces into consideration, that is, not just the three tax fields which they have committed themselves to use as a basis for equalization payments, then they should have taken all the revenues. They should have taken into consideration liquor profits, sales taxes, motor vehicle licence fees and all the other varied sources of revenue which would have been a much fairer criteria of a province's financial position than to take the revenues from natural resources.
There are two other things that are wrong with taking into consideration the revenues from natural resources. The first is that in many instances these are non-recurring revenues. This is particularly true in the case of minerals and petroleum. The province is selling some of its capital assets when minerals are taken out of the ground or when oil and gas are drawn off. This is wealth of which the province is depriving itself. It is selling part of its capital assets and those capital assets, under this new formula, are going to be treated as current revenue.
The other serious defect with regard to treating natural resource revenue as a basis for equalization payments is that the government has overlooked the fact that these revenues are secured as a result of a very heavy provincial expenditure. This is true of provinces such as British Columbia. British Columbia has large forests but it must build access roads, conduct reforestation programs and, above all, be responsible for fire prevention and firefighting programs. If the Minister of Finance feels he really must include resource revenue, surely he ought to take into account net revenue rather than gross revenue. For the federal government to include all revenue from resources when computing these equalization payments seems to me to be grossly unfair and discriminatory against some of the provinces, particularly the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
There is another change in the formula which the minister has never explained to my satisfaction. Why has the additional abatement on the estate tax not been taken into the formula for equalization? On second reading, the minister said when I asked him about this: It is part of the problem of putting together a formula at the end of the day in the dying hours of a federal-provincial con-
Federal-Provincial Relations ference. I find it difficult to accept this as an explanation, because the estates tax abatement is already included in the computation of the equalization payments. The formula prior to this amendment being passed, the formula at the present time, is 18, 9 and 50- 18 percentage points on personal income tax, 9 on corporation tax and 50 on the estates tax. All the federal government had to do was to raise that 50 to 75, and the provinces would be entitled to an abatement of 75 per cent and all of it would have been included when compiling the equalization payments. Here we have the amazing spectacle of two-thirds of the abatement being included for equalization purposes and one third being left out of the equalization formula. This does not make sense. This is not something done in the dying hours of the conference for lack of knowing what to do.
The minister assured us that all the provinces are getting a little more money. Of course they are. The government would not have dared to bring in a formula which did not give all the provinces a little more money. As I said the other day, everybody is equal but some are more equal than others. By taking the additional 25 per cent abatement of estates tax out of the equalization fund, $32,170,000 of additional revenue goes to the provinces. But the provinces of Ontario and Quebec between them get more than $22 million of this in the current fiscal year. In the next fiscal year, the provinces get an additional $33,779,000 and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec get $23 million. And in the final year of the agreement, the provinces are to get an additional $35,408,000 of which the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will get $25 million. So equalization has gone out of the window as far as the distribution of the benefits of this additional 25 per cent abatement on the estates tax is concerned.
I get a little annoyed when I hear ministers rising to rebuke either their own followers or members on the other side of the house on the grounds that the government is in favour of equalization-that this is the lodestar of the Liberal party's program and its chief article of faith-at a time when we are being asked to approve a formula which is regressive, as far as equalization is concerned, with the exception that we are now equalizing to the level of the top two provinces, which is an improvement. But as far as the inclusion of revenue from resource development is concerned, and as far as leaving out the additional 25 per cent abatement on estates tax is concerned, this is a regressive measure. The



Federal-Provincial Relations two provisions I have just mentioned represent a departure from an equalization formula which had been approved by both federal and provincial governments and which is working admirably.
We cannot escape the conclusion that the only reason for making the changes suggested in this formula is to get a desired result. One need only look at the results themselves. In this fiscal year the provinces are to get an extra $87,479,000 of which the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will receive, between them, almost $58 million. Next year, out of $106 million, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will receive some $69 million. Then, in the last year of the agreement, in those two fields, of the $125 million, Ontario and Quebec will get between them some $80 million. It may be that the federal government felt it had to make some concession to the wealthier provinces-that it had to depart from the principle of equalization in certain respects. But if this is to be done, let them not do it on the basis of a suggestion that there was difficulty in formulating an equation which would be satisfactory, for they already have a good equation. The government has changed the formula, in my opinion, because this was the best way by which to pacify those who were finding fault with the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. This represents a serious departure from the principle of equalization.
I think the time will come when the government will regret it has set its feet along this road, because the pressure will continue for doing even greater violence to the principle of equalization. I hope the minister will give us some assurance that if he is not prepared to make some fairly serious changes in this legislation at the present time the government does intend to return to the principles of equalization when negotiations with the provinces are resumed. If it does not, let me say there is nothing which will do more to wreck confederation than for us to have in Canada some parts of the country enjoying high levels of education, welfare and health services while other parts have low incomes, inadequate services, and a feeling they have been forgotten by the federal government and the federal parliament.
I do urge the minister to recognize that this is a retrogressive formula which he has now introduced. This is a departure from the principle of equalization, and I hope he can give us some assurance that we are going to come back as quickly as possible to an ade-

quate equalization formula for federal-provincial fiscal relations.

Mr. Chairman, at the time of adjournment I was referring particularly to the equalization formula that has been produced by the minister. An examination of that formula indicates that it is not based upon any known degree of common sense or logic. It has simply been brought about in order to achieve the objective of the government. Certainly the minister was not able this afternoon to explain the nature of this formula, or give the reason why the percentage arrived at should be one half of the excess over the average of the natural resources income of the various provinces. In other words, it is a formula designed to achieve a result the government had in mind.
At the same time this formula was brought about in a rush. One cannot understand it. It has all the appearances of a shotgun marriage. Certainly it was adopted under circumstances of immediate necessity consequent on the failure of the government to satisfy the provinces at the conference in Quebec. It is unfair, unjust and unscientific in every way.
In so far as British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned, it places upon them a degree of inequity not in keeping with the principle that in all parts of Canada there shall be equal rights and equal responsibility. I should like the minister to give an explanation in this regard. I realize that in asking him to do that I am expecting an explanation of the unexplainable. In answer to questions asked in this connection just before the adjournment he in fact admitted the arbitrary nature of the basis upon which the determination as to equalization is to be made.
I repeat what I said earlier, that this government when in opposition stood for certain principles. It has departed from them. I am not going to repeat that which I dealt with this afternoon in this connection, except to say that it has been noticeable that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Transport have been absent from the house during this debate, no doubt mindful of the fact that, had they been present, quotations would have been used from the speeches they made in 1960 and 1961, which set out principles which were basically the antithesis of the policy now placed before the committee.

speechtext:
Earlier this afternoon when the Minister of Finance replied to some of the questions that were raised immediately preceding his speech by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I thought I detected a note of impatience. He suggested he had already answered the same question four times. He seemed to think he had already supplied an adequate answer to the questions that were raised. So far as I am concerned, he has not as yet given any logical or sensible reason for the way in which clause 4 has been compiled.
As has been pointed out four or five times, Mr. Chairman, the Liberal party, prior to the 1963 election, was committed to setting up equalization on the basis of those taxes that are shared by the two levels of government. Now, Mr. Chairman, natural resource revenue is not a tax that is shared by two levels of government. If memory serves me correctly, and I think it does, the natural resources of this country were turned over to the provinces by the federal government in 1930. Since that time there has been no claim by the federal government on the fruits of development of those natural resources.
In addition to that, during the course of the minister's remarks he said, with respect to the 25 per cent abatement of the estate tax being excluded from the equalization formula at this time, that it did not make sense taken by itself. However, when it was included in the over-all package amendments that are in Bill No. C-lll, he seemed to think there was some justification for it. I should like to draw to your attention that if you take the over-all package amendments that are provided in Bill No. C-lll, there is even more discrimination against the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta than if you take some of the sections one at a time.
For example, clause 5 which we will be considering next provides for sales tax payments by federal crown corporations. Some of the provinces do not collect retail sales taxes.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: That is two years away.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
It may be two years away, but this is one of the points with which I am going to deal. Is the federal government now trying to set up such discriminatory fiscal arrangements between the two levels of government that they intend to force provincial governments to enact legislation they do not wish to enact? I am going to talk about this

Federal-Provincial Relations a good deal when we get to this provision. A clause of this type, when it is taken in the over-all concept of Bill No. C-lll, is simply going to mean there will be bigger federal sums paid to those provinces that levy the highest retail sales tax.
I am more disturbed about some of the other things the minister had to say this afternoon. He said that the arrangements contained in this bill are not perfect. He went farther and said he was not satisfied with the tax arrangements between the two levels of government prior to the introduction of this bill. He hoped that from time to time they would be improved. He has an opportunity now to amend this clause 4 to bring about equalization on the basis of the standard tax fields, rather than introduce other factors such as national resource revenue.
As far as the members from Alberta and British Columbia are concerned we are not pleading poverty when we ask for amendments to clause 4. What we are pleading for is justice. Taking such things as the revenue received from the sale of a capital asset and including them as tax revenue for the purpose of equalization is not justice. We have looked forward to the day when the government would sit down and conscientiously work out a set of principles and ground rules which would govern federal provincial fiscal arrangements, and then apply the formula in fairness to the citizens of all provinces. But in clause 4 we find a continuance or a perpetuation of some of those discriminatory provisions about which protests have been made in the past.
The question has been asked over and over again why such things as gasoline tax, liquor taxes, and so on, were not taken into consideration whereas revenue from natural resources was included. Still we have had no satisfactory answer. Surely the prosperity of a province can better be determined on the basis of such things as liquor tax revenue than by the sale of capital assets in the course of the liquidation of natural resources?
The other day the minister tried to argue that because the province of Alberta includes as revenue receipts from the sale of oil and other natural resources this was tantamount to an admission that they were taxable revenue. I could not disagree more. If the minister were familiar with some of the other ways in which the province of Alberta keeps its books he would, perhaps, find other examples of what he might consider to be abnormal practices compared with those of some of the other provinces. There is at


least another respect in which Alberta bookkeeping might be regarded as a departure from normal practice. We do not separate operating expenses from capital expenditure. It is a fact. It is a fact that every highway, every building and every capital expenditure in Alberta is treated as a current expenditure and paid for in the year in which that expenditure is incurred. Is it now to be necessary for the province to separate the bonuses, and so on, which they receive as a result of the sale of capital assets-I am thinking particularly of the oil and gas leases-and place them in a separate account as capital receipts rather than as revenue, in other words to set up two sets of books for accounting purposes so that all these things do not get into the revenue side? If discrimination of this kind is to be continued it will, in fact, constitute an intrusion upon the manner in which the government of Alberta chooses to run its affairs. There are ways round this, should it become necessary to take them. I certainly hope the Canadian government will not continue this kind of discrimination until it becomes necessary to change some of our accounting methods in order to obtain some kind of justice.
The government has still not explained why it should take into account the gross amount of revenue received from the sales of capital resources rather than the net amount derived from these sources. No provision is made for the expense of developing these resources. Instead, the gross income is taken and, as yet, there has been no explanation why this should be so.
There are one or two other things which the minister had to say this evening and upon which I should like to comment. I think he laughed a little at some of the ways in which the province of British Columbia chose to keep its accounts. He sneered, if I may use that term, though perhaps mildly, at the claim of the premier of British Columbia that the province was now debt free as far as debt held in the name of the province was concerned. The minister may laugh at that if he likes but I will tell him one of the facts of life as far as British Columbia is concerned: There is no levy on the citizens of British Columbia now, to pay debt services on any provincial debt. Whether he likes that fact of life or not, it is true, and in case he is not aware of it, let me tell him that the two provinces of Alberta and British Columbia have experienced the highest rate of growth during the last ten or 15 years of any provinces in Canada. There has been

a movement of people from all over Canada into those two provinces. This is indicative of a growing economy, and whether the minister cares to refer to it in jest or not is a matter for him to decide. Nevertheless these are the facts of life.
We cannot accept the reasons which have been given so far for producing a formula of the kind now advocated as a basis for re-arranging the agreements between the provinces for sharing tax revenue. We cannot understand why certain taxes were excluded. As a matter of fact, when we talk about standard taxes-and this phrase is used several times in the various subclauses of clause 4-it seems to me that every province in Canada levies a liquor tax and that every province levies a gasoline tax. These are taxes which could properly be included among the standard taxes. Instead, the taxes which were consistent, or reasonably consistent, from province to province were ignored and the government included such things as the gross revenue from the sale of natural resources.
As has been pointed out time and time again, and as the minister himself stated, as will be seen if we turn to page 5282 of Hansard, this natural resource revenue per capita ranges from a low of 15 cents in Prince Edward Island to a high of $94.08 in Alberta. It is becoming more and more obvious as a result of the interrogation which has been carried on while this bill has been before parliament that the amount of money which the federal government was pressured if I may use that word, into distributing to the provinces was a predetermined figure and then the formula was concocted in order to meet that figure. Why? Why increase the percentage points of abatement of succession duties or estates tax and then exempt one-third of that from the tax equalization calculations? The minister gave us a most unsatisfactory answer when he told us that though this might not seem very logical in itself it became more reasonable, or more logical, when considered in the light of the whole package. This answer is a further indication that the amount which the federal government wanted to give to each of the provinces was predetermined and that the formula was cooked up to meet this figure.
I have no desire to prolong this debate unduly. In so far as British Columbia and Alberta are concerned, we are not being treated fairly and we are pleading for some justice in the formula. The attitude of both governments has been over the years that we 20220-423
Federal-Provincial Relations are part of confederation and that it shall be an obligation on certain provinces, when their economy is buoyant, to assist other regions in the country that are perhaps lagging, and we hope lagging temporarily. But, Mr. Chairman while the two provinces have acknowledged this, we think there should be, as I have said before, a formula set down, a set of principles and a set of ground rules laid down, and these should be made to apply to all provinces.
The table the minister gave to the house on July 7, which is to be found at page 5184 of Hansard, clearly indicates that the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, under changes in the equalization formula, when they occur next year, to 18-9-50 will receive no additional payments. The reason is the inclusion of half the natural resource revenue. When the next change comes about during the fiscal year 1965-66, the equalization formula will be changed to 19-9-50, but in that year too there will be no additional distribution of tax revenues to the two western provinces. Again, in 1966-67, when the formula is changed again to 20-9-50, there will be absolutely no increase under the equalization formula for either British Columbia or Alberta. I do not believe we can continue to reel, as I said the other day, from one temporary improvisation to another to satisfy the expedient of the day. It is not good business; it is not sound for these formulas to be based on which province can make the most noise.
We accept equalization on the basis of helping those areas in Canada that are lagging economically behind others, but we do not like to have the formula cooked to such an extent that there are serious injustices being committed, such as we see here. We would like to have the minister tell us why the liquor tax, the gasoline tax and some of these other taxes that are pretty universal across the country were ignored when the government considered provincial revenues. We would like to have a considerably better answer as to why the additional 25 points in the estate tax is not to be considered, unless this is some kind of a sop or concession to certain provinces in order to have them give in on other changes in the formula. As far as I am concerned, clause 4 is not satisfactory; it is unjust and discriminatory, and we do not believe that proceeding on this kind of basis is doing Canada any good.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not for one moment share the political views of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Nor do I make myself, as he might try to do, an apologist for the Alberta government, whose political philosophies the hon. member for Medicine Hat might attempt to espouse. I must say however, I do have some sympathy for some of those principles he has enunciated tonight.
I apologize to the committee for repeating myself. Notwithstanding the minister's repetition of the legal definition of section 2(c) of chapter 58, of the Statutes of Canada, 1960-61, defining natural resources revenue, I find myself as a graduate of commerce, accountancy and business administration, in some difficulty in reconciling actual fact with this legal definition. I am sure the minister would find the same difficulty.
I admit at the outset that Alberta, and British Columbia to a lesser degree, may be wearing a self-fashioned hairshirt at this time. Because of their own political desires and motivations they have seen fit to lump together capital receipts and revenues in the natural resources field. The hon. member for Medicine Hat, as well as myself and others, have made a distinction in this regard. I think also the government formerly headed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam also lumped these items together so far as natural resources were concerned.
I think these governments have committed a factual and economic blunder. I do not think they should have considered these things together. I feel there must be a clear distinction made between capital receipts and revenues from natural resources. I am sure had those governments treated receipts and revenues on different terms, and fashioned their spending programs and budgets in this way, we would not now be faced with this

problem. Had such an attitude been taken I am sure we would now have ample corroborating evidence to counter any argument put forward by the federal government.
I am the first to admit that this natural resources revenue was brought into an equalization formula in 1961 under an administration I supported. That situation does not negate the fact that I objected to it at that time. The province of Alberta at that time was the only province adversely affected. The one argument I and others could not counter had relation to the fact that under the 1957 agreement, which classified Alberta as a have-not province, which was in existence in 1958 and 1959 the provincial administration saw fit to declare dividends to the extent of $11 million or $12 million each year. The province of Alberta was receiving payments to the extent of $17 million or $18 million from the federal government at that time. This created an inexplicable position.
I remember attempting to support this situation during a discussion with my colleagues, but counter-supporting facts just were not in existence. So long as Alberta was classified as a have-not province and at the same time was declaring a preposterous dividend, there were no grounds for argument. Because of this silly political nonsense on the part of the Social Credit party in the province of Alberta we here in Ottawa, who had real grounds for argument in respect of this division between capital receipts and revenues from natural resources, lost a great deal of ground.
I should like to remind hon. members that Alberta's prosperity resulted from a rather unnatural situation. It resulted from conditions which existed during the Korean war and following the Suez crisis. Let me assure all hon. members of this house, including those from Alberta, that if conditions such as those which existed following the Suez crisis recurred, keeping in mind the fact that Alberta is presently on the eve of developing the tar sands, the revenues of the last decade could appear picayune when compared with the revenues which could accrue to the provincial administration during the forthcoming decade. This is as sure as the sun will rise tomorrow. These are economic facts. Alberta has been fortunate. I do not intend to apologize for the citizens of Alberta, but I should like to remind everyone that God placed the oil and gas under the soil of the plains, foothills and mountains of Alberta, and man found them at the appropriate time.

In the course of his reply to the hon. member for Medicine Hat regarding the financial position of British Columbia, he said that if any province reaches the state where it is debt free, in the true sense of the word, that would be a cause for rejoicing. I noticed, sir, that he inserted that little word "if". I do not believe the Minister of Finance read the editorial in the Financial Times of Friday, August 7, 1959. I believe that for his enlightenment and edification it might be interesting if we put it on the record tonight. This editorial refers to the time when the premier of British Columbia set fire to certain cancelled bonds in the interior of British Columbia. I quote:
Perhaps the showmanship on the occasion of B.C.'s bond burning last week was extravagant but the achievement was real.
When Premier W. A. C. Bennett of British Columbia, in an elaborate ritual, consigned some $70 million of cancelled bonds to the fire, thus wiping out the balance of the province's direct debt which stood at $191 million seven years ago, he accomplished something which taxpayers all over Canada wish could be done in the name of their own provinces (and of Ottawa too).
But polities creates strange moods. There has been an extraordinary amount of carping; charges of trickery have been raised and fingers are pointed at the indirect or contingent debt of the province. The critics have really made hay out of their disapproval of the Bennett claims, although they are on very poor ground indeed.
There is a difference, a very real difference, between direct and contingent debts; between debts the service of which is a direct charge on all

Federal-Provincial Relations
g&vernment revenues on the one hand, and debts which are largely, or wholly, self-sustaining occasionally even self-amortizing, such as the bonds issued by provincial power commissions, toll highway commissions and similar government agencies.
An indirect provincial debt is simply one the service of which is guaranteed by the province in the unlikely event that a power commission, etc., would default on its own obligations.
In times of generally rising government direct debts and the steady growth of interest requirements on such debts, one would have thought that B.C.'s achievement would have been greeted with serious interest. However, the fact that it was done by a government that happens to label itself "Social Credit" was enough to bring out venom and ridicule.
It is said that substantial sales taxes were needed to retire the debt. But at least these taxes did have this result. We note very high sales taxes ift other provinces (and in Ottawa) without any evidence that a similar result is even contemplated. This is one instance where emulation rather than carping is definitely in order.
X see the Minister of Finance has been able to return to the house. I hope he will take time to read this statement that has been put an the record. Even though the Minister of Finance may deny the fact, and even though some of the other critics may deny the fact, yet those in financial circles recognize the fact and acknowledge it. I think possibly a little honesty would be of value in the consideration of this matter. The Minister of Finance, replying to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat that the government of Alberta might have to make some changes in its accounting procedures, said he did not believe any self-respecting government would do such a thing. May I say-perhaps I should-that no self-respecting federal government would act in the way this one is doing in this particular instance. Are we reaching a point where a federal government is continuing to crowd the western provinces into a corner every time? Then they wonder why it is we take exception to their actions and to their legislation. They did it when the premier of British Columbia asked that the utility corporations be exempted from corporation tax in the same way as crown corporations are. He was met with refusal on every hand until he was forced into the position where, in order to give the consumers a fair deal, he had to take action. This legislation appears to be following the same course. Once again the federal government is crowding us into a corner and refusing even to give a satisfactory explanation Why they are doing it. As the hon. member for Edmonton West has said, the question has been raised by members from various parts of the country but no satisfactory reason has

been given why the government, in the words of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, should have cooked up this formula which militates against the best interests of two of the western provinces and perhaps the three, as is being suggested.
The hon. member for Edmonton West says the government out there cannot take credit for the natural resources which are being developed. That is true. But I believe they can take a measure of credit for the fact that they have been developed and administered in such a way that the province has benefited from them. The same situation obtains in the province of British Columbia. We all know the problems which were faced there prior to 1952 and we know what has transpired since that time. The present government there does not take credit for the fact that the resources are available to the province, but I believe the people of the province give the government credit for seeing that they were developed and are being developed in the best interests of British Columbia.
As I said the other day, I find it difficult to understand why certain members of this house continue to downgrade their own provinces. Just the other day, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-I am glad he is here tonight-said that the premier of British Columbia was one of the greatest separatists he knew. I would like him to prove that. I do not believe he could. I know charges are thrown around wildly without any basis in fact, and this is one of them. I should like to call attention to the report of the federal-provincial conference in 1963. The conclusion of the representations made by the province of British Columbia, as reported on page 71 reads as follows:
Certainly we offer these proposals In the interests of British Columbia but we do so confident that our proposals will help all of Canada to grow and prosper, for we, like all Canadians, are citizens first of a country and not of a province.
That does not sound like separatism. So I trust the Minister of Finance will take some of these matters under advisement, give consideration to the statements which have been made and come up at least with an answer, if not with changes in this formula so as to bring it more in line with reality.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
The
committee will perhaps forgive me if I do not indulge in any further exploration of the labyrinth of British Columbia debt accounting, but if I return to the clause now under

consideration, clause 4, and in particular this
provision:
(5) (a) the amount by which the average per capita natural resources revenues of the province for the three fiscal years immediately preceding the fiscal year exceed the average per capita natural resources revenues of all the provinces for the three fiscal years immediately preceding the fiscal year.
As has been indicated by other speakers in this discussion, we are seeking simply to secure from the minister some undertaking that he will consider the inequity which exists in this clause. Perhaps a provision of this general nature has existed for many years in our tax arrangements with the provinces. But it is not desirable to perpetuate this arrangement if it can be proved there is a fundamental weakness attached to it. My suggestion to the minister tonight is that there is a fundamental weakness here. I would ask him to indicate to the committee that he is prepared to accept the fact that there must be some differentiation between true natural resource income and the sale of a capital asset.
If you are gaining an income from a renewable resource-from a forest resource, for instance, which can be sustained and made to yield a continuing revenue-it can properly be regarded as income. But if you are receiving revenue resulting from the sale of an asset-gold, iron, silver, copper, any of the minerals, which cannot by any policy of management be restored; if you are obtaining revenue derived from the sale of oil or natural gas, which cannot, by any exercise of management be renewed; once it is gone, it is gone for good-an entirely different consideration arises. This is what I ask the Minister of Finance to recognize. I am sure this is what many members who have spoken over the past several days are seeking from him. Just as in the field of federal taxation capital gains are not taxed, we should not take these capital gains into account in an equalization formula, but rather we should recognize that the only income which should be taken into account under such a formula is that which is renewable and can be perpetuated. That is all I ask of the minister. I ask him to take this principle into account.
To summarize; Natural resource income is that income which derives from a resource which can be perpetuated, whereas revenue from the sale of resources which are not renewable amount to the sale of an asset and should be considered as a capital gain.

speechtext:
When I heard the hon. member for Fraser Valley reading an editorial from the Financial Times I was tempted to

In reference to the latter part of the hon. member's remarks, in which he took some umbrage at my suggestion that the premier of British Columbia exhibits separatist tendencies, I would remind the hon. member that when I made those references I quoted from the same statement to which he referred. But I find myself less concerned with the fine sounding phrases in the peroration of the submission of the premier of British Columbia than with what I consider to be the meat of the submission. At that earlier stage I pointed out that the premier's statement was to the effect-and I am quoting from page 69-that "British Columbia is opposed to federal equalization grants to the provinces. Equalization does not contribute to national harmony or efficient use of public moneys". In my own view-and I recognize this is a matter of opinion-anyone who holds those views, considering the realities of the Canadian federation, is in fact advocating a policy of separatism as I have come to understand it.
I also made reference to the fact that in my view the premier in his submission has done much as he has done before, namely attempt to distort the constitution as it is contained in the British North America Act. I did not at that time spell out my contention, but the premier in his submission makes the claim that direct taxation is assigned, under the British North America Act, as the exclusive prerogative of the provinces. I sub-

Federal-Provincial Relations mit that is a distortion of the constitution, and anyone who would attempt to do that is exhibiting the tendencies which I described as separatist. It is true that direct taxation is listed in section 92 as one of the prerogatives of the provinces; but I would like to point out that in section 91, where are set out the powers of the parliament of Canada with regard to legislation, it says, if I may quote in part:
-but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms in this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated-
Then No. 3 is:
The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
My submission is that the premier of British Columbia cannot have said these things inadvertently, considering his knowledge and experience, and he has tried to suggest in his submission something which is simply not correct as far as the constitution is concerned. I would also point out that earlier today the hon. member for Villeneuve quoted this particular statement of the premier of British Columbia in reference to the British North America Act and the powers of taxation. He quoted it with a good deal of approval as in effect bolstering the argument he was advancing in this house. I did take pains to point out to the hon. member for Villeneuve later, informally, that he should not always take at face value statements of that kind when they were made by the premier of British Columbia, because thereby he was being led into a serious error and misunderstanding with regard to our constitution. In effect the hon. member for Villeneuve was attempting to use this statement to bolster his argument in favour of the positions taken at the recent convention of the Ralliement Cre-ditiste in the province of Quebec. Therefore I think that when one finds that kind of relationship perhaps my claim of separatist tendencies, which I consider dangerous to the well-being of the Canadian federation, is not without foundation.

An hon. member says it leads to bankruptcy. It certainly has led to discriminatory action in regard to equalization and taxation, as they are applied to the province of Alberta. I thank the hon. member for Edmonton West and I hope some of his colleagues in the Conservative party from the province of Alberta will follow his example in rising in the house on an occasion such as this and standing up for the people of the province of Alberta when we see this discriminatory kind of legislation before the house. I commend him for doing that and I hope, as I have said, that his other Progressive Conservative colleagues from Alberta will do the same; because all too often in this house we have seen some of the members from the province of Alberta take great delight in downgrading their province. We do not think this is proper.
To get back to the point I was trying to make with the Minister of Finance, there have been occasions when the right to develop proven oil areas, areas in which there are proven reserves, have been offered for sale in the province of Alberta. On more than one occasion this has been done by way of a bonus, or whatever you want to call it, to the tune of $10,000 per acre. In fact, in one case I remember, just the right to a lease to develop the area for a 20-year period was sold for $16,000 an acre. That is not a recurring revenue. That sale gave the right to the oil company, or the individual-whoever bought it-to develop that area over a period of time as laid down in the terms of the lease. It is not fair to consider that to be an ordinary current revenue.
The minister says that no self-respecting province would set up a capital account in which to put these kinds of funds, to separate them from recurring or ordinary current revenue. I hope the federal government are not on a course that is going to force the province of Alberta and other provinces to do this kind of thing. To get back to the point in

question, Mr. Chairman, there have been numerous representations from members in this house that the federal government ought to take into consideration such things as the sale of capital assets, net revenue from natural resources rather than gross revenue, and cost of administration. In my view that is the difference between gross and net. However, so far the minister has not given any indication that he is willing to take these things into consideration.
Let me now lay down three suggestions which in all fairness ought to be taken into consideration. First of all, natural resource revenue is not a tax shared by the two levels of government. If I understand the basic premise on which equalization is based, it is that there shall be a redistribution of the so-called standard taxes referred to a number of times in this bill. These standard taxes consist of personal income tax, corporation income tax and estate tax. These taxes are levied at the same level, or near the same level, all over Canada. These taxes are levied at nearly the same rate all over the country. In some areas where the amount of money received from these standard taxes falls below a certain level I think the equalization principle and formula is fair and just. But I do not believe that natural resource revenue ought to be included because it is not levied at the same rate in all provinces. The other provinces have the right, if they choose, to impose royalties on the production of nickel, timber and all the other minerals which are produced. But if they do not happen to choose to do that there is no sound logic in penalizing those provinces who do claim a fair and just portion of the production of natural resources and minerals in their provinces.
If the government completely rejects this proposal that natural resources revenue should be excluded, surely they should be willing to accept a differentiation between the sale of capital assets and current revenue or royalties. So far there has been no indication that they are willing to recognize that some of the money which now gets into current account in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan is in fact from the sale of a capital asset.
The third point concerns the difference between net and gross. Even though you consider only the current recurring revenue which comes from the development and exploitation of natural resources in those provinces where this current revenue has reached high levels, you must also remember that along with it have come high levels of ex-20220-424J

It has been pointed out time and again that so far as timber is concerned the province of British Columbia in particular spends millions and millions of dollars on the protection of forests and has programs to ensure the continuity of forest production in the province. In the province of Alberta there is the oil and gas conservation board and a rather large force of administrative personnel to see to it that the natural gas and oil is developed in such a way that we will have optimum production from these reserves. We think that this is unfair. So far all the minister is able to say is that there was an arbitrary figure reached of 50 per cent, which is above the national average, and he has not given any logical reason why this arbitrary figure was arrived at.
With regard to the point about the difference between gross and net, when you consider the other three so-called standard taxes -income tax, corporation tax and estate tax -outside of a very small percentage of that tax, which amount is required to meet the expenses of the personnel who collect it, it is net. I suggest that the higher the natural resources level in a given province, there is along with it a proportionately higher level of cost to maintain these resources. That is the point of principle. Having agreed to the principle I presume that my hon. friend is only objecting now to making it retroactive to the time that the commitment was made. If I may say so, I do not believe that this is the appropriate time to raise the question of principle involved which was settled when the Crown Corporations (Provincial Taxes and Fees) Act was passed. That has been dealt with and we are done with it. All we are doing now is to provide authority to make comparable payments from the beginning of the time when the commitment was made.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to take exception to what the Minister of Finance has just said and I would refer him to page 3239 of Hansard when the Crown Corporations (Provincial Taxes and Fees) Act was passed by the House of Commons. On that occasion I took very strong exception-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member for Medicine Hat did. In fact, I remember his doing it. However, despite his representations the house decided to approve the legislation and therefore I suggest with respect that the matter is not debatable again.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at that time I asked some questions about what the government was going to do to equalize and be fair to those provinces that do not levy a sales tax. To put the matter in its proper context I think I should read part of the statement that the Minister of Finance made in the house on July 7 last. As found on page 5186 of Hansard he said at that time:
While it was thought wrong at this time to give retroactive effect to this legislation-
The legislation for the payment of these fees.
-the government does not want the provinces to lose financially-I am referring to the bill that was passed some weeks ago-
I presume that is the bill which was passed on May 13.
-from the fact that events over which they had no control intervened in such a way as to make it impossible to carry out the original intention. It was more than an intention; it was more or less a commitment. Consequently it is proposed that an estimate be made of the taxes that would have been paid had the legislation been in effect
[Mr. Gordon.J
from April 1, 1962 to March 31, 1964 and that such estimated amounts be paid to the provinces. It will come to about $6 million in total for the two years in question.
I believe it was the parliamentary secretary who was answering for the minister on May 13 and at that time I asked him what the government was going to do about those provinces that do not levy sales taxes. I asked him if they were prepared to pay grants in lieu of such taxes on the basis of estimating the amount they would have received if they had had a sales tax in effect. I quote the question I asked at that time, as found on page 3239 of Hansard:
Has any consideration been given to making cash payments to those provinces which do not levy sales tax, in lieu of tax revenue from these corporations?
The answer of the then parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, now Minister of National Revenue, was as follows:
No consideration has been given to this matter. It would be extremely difficult-
Note these words.
-to calculate how much revenue would have been realized had a sales tax been imposed-
Now the government turns a complete somersault. They said on May 13 that it would be extremely difficult to calculate the amount of tax to arrive at the amount of cash grant in lieu of such a tax, but now they come forward with clause 5 of Bill No. C-lll and say that they are going to make an estimate of the taxes that would have been paid had the legislation been in effect since April 1, 1962.
In almost every case where certain provinces have decided not to participate in the operation of some piece of federal legislation the federal government has made provision to grant them a cash payment in lieu of what the taxes might have been on the one hand, or on the other hand in other cases on the basis of how much it would have cost the federal government had the particular program been accepted and made operative in that province. We can refer, for example, to youth allowances. We can refer to the cost of loans to students. Payments are going to be made to any province that chooses to opt out and not participate with the federal government in the program. In those cases it is possible for the Minister of Finance and his department to calculate the amount of the cash grant in lieu of participation. Why is it not possible in this case where crown corporations are involved and an indirect tax out of the federal treasury? Why are

certain provinces being denied a cash grant in lieu of the taxes that they might have collected? To make the situation even worse, the government is now going to go back and make this provision retroactive for two years.
The Minister of National Revenue stated that they could not calculate what the amount would be in the case of provinces that do not levy such a sales tax now, but now the Minister of Finance says that a recapitulation is going to be made of all this potential tax revenue for the past two years as if in fact the legislation passed on May 13 had been in effect. There is more to the matter than that. What is going to happen from now on if these taxes and fees are going to be paid by crown corporations? Are directives going to be issued to crown corporations that they must make their purchases in certain provinces? If you want to take the two extremes of Alberta and Manitoba as opposed to Quebec, certainly when tenders are called-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, surely we should stick to the subject before the committee.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: I cannot believe, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is objecting to the relevancy of my remarks.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: He is not enjoying them.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: He may not be enjoying them, but certainly I am talking now about what is going to happen in connection with the administration of this measure. We are considering clause 5 if the minister is not aware of that. This is a matter of collecting provincial taxes from crown corporations. The point I tried to make, Mr. Chairman, was that there would be a 6 per cent difference in the amount of tenders, for example, from the province of Quebec as opposed to those from the provinces of Manitoba or Alberta. Is the federal government going to insist-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: I wonder if I might rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman? I do not see how the question of tenders could possibly come into this matter when we are talking about a retroactive payment for two years. We are not talking now about the future or the present, we are just talking about the past. So far as I am aware, no tenders are going to be called retroactively back to 1962.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
It appears to the Chair that the last two or three sentences of the hon. member's remarks seem to be getting away from clause 5 which, as he knows, is the subject matter of the discussion before the
Federal-Provincial Relations committee. He knows also that in committee discussion must be strictly relevant to the clause before us. On the other hand, in so far as the Chair could judge, before those last few remarks the hon. member appeared to be relevant. I know he will keep this in mind in continuing his remarks.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
I appreciate your guidance in this matter, Mr. Chairman. I point out to you, sir, that on a number of occasions in the past I have tried to get some information from the minister as to what is going to happen after federal crown corporations are required to pay provincial sales taxes. So far the minister has not said what is going to happen with respect to the discrepancy between the cost of purchasing supplies. Obviously, there is going to be a 6 per cent differential between some provinces for exactly the same article, if it is being sold for the same price. We have had no explanation from him in this respect.
I am asking him now, are there going to be directives go forward in connection with this matter to insist that crown corporations in Saskatchewan, for example, must buy their supplies in the province of Saskatchewan? Is the government going to grant a measure of tolerance to crown corporations to take care of this differential? If they do not, then Manitoba and Alberta are certainly going to be in preferred positions when it comes to tendering on supplies for crown corporations. We have had no answer so far, Mr. Chairman. I think I am dealing specifically with matters related to the payment of provincial taxes by crown corporations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: It seems to the Chair that the hon. member is really talking about the operations of a provision of a prior bill. It seems to me that, even though there is a reference in this clause to the prior bill, this does not open for discussion the details of the previous legislation.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
As has been pointed out to me, Mr. Chairman, we are amending that previous bill now. This previous bill was passed on May 13, as I understand it, and is now up for amendment to the extent that this provision is being made retroactive for two years. This is a major amendment, and inasmuch as that is the case surely we have the right to ask the minister questions about the practical application of this measure. I still maintain, with deference to you sir, that when we are considering a measure amending this

Federal-Provincial Relations previous bill, we should have some answers to the questions that have been asked.
There is one other thing I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman. I hope the Minister of Finance is going to answer those last two questions. I should like him to explain also what has happened to the principle that one government should not be in a position to tax another, that is one level of government should not be in a position to tax another level of government. As has been pointed out on a number of occasions, this Crown Corporations (Provincial Taxes and Fees) Act is going to allow the provinces to gain a larger share of the distribution of funds from the federal treasury by increasing provincial taxes. In many respects this is a violation of some of the concepts of equalization. The equalization formula we have been discussing contains a provision concerning payments to provinces when their level of taxation does not come up to that of other provinces. Prior to the introduction of this bill, that level was the national average. While the provisions of this clause may not be a matter of major concern in terms of absolute dollars, there is in fact a complete contradiction of that principle. As I said before, bonuses are going to be paid to those provinces that levy the highest sales taxes. I hope the Minister of Finance, even though he may not like having these questions put to him, will try to answer them so that the members of this committee can have some indication how the provision is going to be applied in practice.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Definitions.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: In so far as this clause is concerned, paragraph (a), what province to date has indicated it is not going to participate in the youth program under the Youth Allowances Act?

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: The province of Quebec.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: And no others?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext: No.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 7 agreed to.
On clause 8-Regulations.

maintopic: FIRST ESTIMATE OF PAYMENTS AND ABATEMENTS UNDER THE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT 1961
speechtext:
I must register a caveat about the wording in this clause dealing with regulations which, in effect, give carte blanche to the minister to determine these regulations and the carrying into effect of the intent of the regulations. As I indicated on a previous occasion, I draw attention to this and I must

ask the minister and his colleagues to really look at this provision because, frankly, it does give carte blanche to the administration.

speechtext: A motion to adjourn the house under provisional standing order 39A deemed to have been moved:

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO OLYMPIC
FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO OLYMPIC
FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO OLYMPIC
speechtext:
I do not wish to take up the time of the house for very long at this late hour. However, this afternoon I asked a question on the orders of the day which I am sure was of interest to many thousands of Canadians. Since I had sent the minister notice, and since she appeared ready to answer, I thought it only fair to give her or her parliamentary secretary an opportunity to reply tonight.
My question was: "In view of the fact that Olympic trials in track and field were completed last week end in Quebec, to what extent does the federal government plan to contribute toward the cost of sending Canadian athletes to Tokyo later this year?"
There is widespread interest in all kinds of amateur sports in this country including the contests that find a place on the Olympic program. We must remember that the young people who qualify to attend the games do not represent local communities alone, or even

individual provinces. They represent Canada. When they appear in the opening parade in Tokyo, they will march as Canadian ambassadors abroad. That is why I am certain the people of this country will approve any action which the federal government may take to share the cost involved in this worthy project.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO OLYMPIC
speechtext:
I am sure the government shares the sentiments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Webster). The position at the present time is that the Canadian Olympic Association, through the fitness and amateur sports program, has requested and received $122,905 to assist in sending Canadian athletes to the 1964 Olympic games. This amount covers assistance for both the winter games in Innsbruck last January and February and
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the summer games in Tokyo this coming October.
The number of competitors in each event is set by the board of directors of the Canadian Olympic Association in each case. The competitors themselves are selected by the sports governing body in the various Olympic sports.
It might be of interest to note that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) attended the Olympic trials in St. Lambert, Quebec, last Friday with the member for Longueuil (Mr. Cote), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was there for the Saturday events. Also, Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will be pleased to hear that the hon. member for York West (Mr. Kelly) has agreed to represent Canada officially at the Tokyo games.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.34 p.m.
